image_caption: "Terracotta, wet mix and big plants add up fast. The weight is the part of balcony gardening nobody shows you."

faq:
  - q: "How much weight can an apartment balcony hold?"
    a: "Current building codes based on the International Building Code design exterior balconies for the same live load as the rooms they serve, 40 pounds per square foot for private areas of multifamily buildings. That is a design minimum for evenly spread weight, not a promise about your balcony. Only the building's drawings or a structural engineer can say more."
  - q: "How much does a 5-gallon pot of soil weigh when wet?"
    a: "Roughly 30 to 45 pounds with a peat-based potting mix watered until it drains, plus the weight of the pot. A mix that contains garden soil weighs a good deal more. Weigh one pot on a bathroom scale after a thorough watering to get a number for your own containers."
  - q: "Is it safe to put large planters on a balcony?"
    a: "Usually yes, if you keep the heaviest ones against the building wall, spread them out rather than clustering them, and stay well inside the balcony's total design load. Ask the building manager or super before adding anything large, because many leases and building rules limit planters, especially on the railing."
  - q: "Where is the strongest part of a balcony for heavy pots?"
    a: "Against the wall where the balcony meets the building, which is the supported edge of a cantilevered balcony, or beside the posts of a post-supported one. The Royal Horticultural Society says heavy containers belong near load-bearing walls or over a beam or joist. The outer edge and the middle of the span are the weakest places."
  - q: "What is the lightest potting mix for a balcony?"
    a: "A soilless mix of peat or coir with perlite or vermiculite. University of Maryland Extension puts soilless media at about 10 pounds per cubic foot dry, against about 75 for soil. University of Wisconsin Extension recommends soilless mixes when many containers sit on a balcony where excess weight can be a problem."
  - q: "Do I need to tell my landlord about a balcony garden?"
    a: "Read the lease first; many leases and condo rules already say what the balcony may hold and whether anything may hang from the railing. Telling the super or management before you add large containers protects you if a neighbor complains about drips or a pot in the wind, and it is the only way to learn the balcony's load limit."
---

This guide is for the apartment gardener with a balcony, terrace or roof deck, where the limit is not light but weight. A balcony is a slab or a deck hanging off the side of a building, and a vegetable garden in big pots is heavy, wet and permanent.

Here is what a wet planter actually weighs, what the code assumes the balcony carries, where heavy pots should sit, and how to cut the weight. For sun hours, wind and pot sizes by crop, start with [the best vegetables to grow on a balcony](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/).

## How much does a wet planter weigh?

A wet planter weighs several times what the empty pot and the bag of mix suggest, because water is the heavy part. The University of Maryland Extension's guide to [growing vegetables in containers](https://www.extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-vegetables-containers-and-salad-tables) says a 20-inch container filled with moist potting mix and plants can weigh 100 pounds. A gallon of water weighs about 8.3 pounds, and a thorough watering leaves a lot of it in the mix.

The table gives rough working figures for a peat-based mix watered until it drains, plus a plastic pot. They are estimates, not measurements of your pots, so weigh one container on a bathroom scale after watering.

| Container | Mix it holds | Rough weight, wet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small pot, about 2 gallons | 0.3 cubic feet | 15 to 25 pounds |
| 5-gallon bucket or pot | 0.7 cubic feet | 30 to 45 pounds |
| 10-gallon tub | 1.3 cubic feet | 60 to 90 pounds |
| 20-inch pot, about 15 gallons | 2 cubic feet | about 100 pounds |
| 2 by 3 foot planter, 10 inches deep | 5 cubic feet | 250 to 400 pounds |

Terracotta, ceramic and concrete pots add their own weight on top, and a mix with garden soil in it weighs far more. Maryland Extension puts soil at about 75 pounds per cubic foot against about 10 for dry soilless media. Four warm-season vegetables in 5-gallon pots plus one melon tub weigh roughly as much as two adults, standing there all summer.

## How much weight can a balcony hold?

US building codes commonly design a residential balcony for 40 pounds per square foot, spread evenly over the whole surface. The current International Building Code table sets exterior balconies and decks at the same live load as the occupancy they serve. For private rooms in multifamily buildings that is 40 pounds per square foot, as in Massachusetts' [copy of Table 1607.1](https://regulations.justia.com/states/massachusetts/780-cmr/chapter-16/section-1607/subsection-1607-1).

The same table designs a roof used as a roof garden for 100 pounds per square foot, while an ordinary roof is not designed for people and pots. A 4 by 8 foot balcony at 40 pounds per square foot is designed for about 1,280 pounds spread across all 32 square feet. That total includes you, your guests and the furniture, not just the garden.

Treat the code figure as a design minimum, not as your balcony's real capacity. Older code editions asked more of balconies, and local amendments, the building's age, water damage and the way the balcony is supported all change the answer. The building's drawings say what was designed, and only a structural engineer can confirm what a particular balcony will carry today.

## Where should heavy pots sit on a balcony?

Heavy pots belong against the wall where the balcony meets the building, spread out rather than clustered. The Royal Horticultural Society's advice on [roof gardens and balconies](https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/profile?PID=674) says heavy containers should be placed near load-bearing walls or over a load-bearing beam or joist. On a cantilevered balcony, the kind with no posts underneath, the building wall is the supported edge and the outer railing is the free end.

The horticulturist Stephen Albert makes the same point in his [balcony and rooftop garden basics](https://harvesttotable.com/balcony-and-rooftop-vegetable-garden-basics/): balconies are often suspended from the building and cannot bear heavy weight. On a balcony carried by posts, the corners beside the posts are the strong spots. The middle of the span and a cluster of big tubs at the outer edge are the places to avoid.

Keep pots off the railing unless the building allows it and the bracket is rated for a full, wet box, because a planter over a sidewalk is a falling hazard. Never put pots on a fire escape, because it is an emergency exit and blocking it breaks fire code in most cities.

## How do you lighten a balcony container garden?

Switch to a soilless mix, lighter pots and the smallest container each crop actually needs. The University of Wisconsin Extension's [container gardening guide](https://barron.extension.wisc.edu/files/2023/02/Container-Gardening-1.pdf) recommends soilless mixes where many containers sit on a balcony or similar structure and excess weight can be a problem. Peat or coir with perlite or vermiculite is light when dry and still lighter than soil when wet.

Fabric grow bags, plastic and resin pots weigh a fraction of terracotta or concrete, and Maryland Extension notes that fabric bags are lightweight and portable. Skip the layer of gravel in the bottom of the pot, because it adds weight without improving drainage. Empty saucers after watering so you are not storing gallons of water on the slab.

Then size each pot to the crop instead of buying the biggest tub on the shelf. Maryland Extension's minimum volumes run from half a gallon for beets to 5 gallons for standard tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and eggplant. Bigger pots hold more water and crop more reliably, but every gallon of mix above the minimum is weight the balcony carries all season.

| Crop in the Happy Seeds kit | Weight on the balcony | Where to put it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kale, spinach, turnip, beet | Light; several share one planter | Anywhere, or indoors on a sunny sill |
| Carrot | Medium; a 12-inch-deep pot holds more mix | Near the wall, or indoors |
| Pepper | Medium | Mid-balcony is fine |
| Tomato, eggplant, cucumber | Heavy once staked, trellised and watered | Against the building wall |
| Melon | Heaviest single pot, 10 gallons or more | At the wall, never at the outer edge |

## What do the lease and the building rules say about planters?

Read the lease, the house rules or the condo bylaws before buying a single pot, because many already limit what a balcony may hold. Common rules cover planters on or over the railing, drip onto the balcony below, and a weight limit that management will quote if you ask. A note to the super that you are adding large containers costs nothing and starts the conversation about the load limit.

Neighbors matter as much as rules. Water that runs out of a 10-gallon tub lands on the balcony below, so keep a tray under anything large. A trellis or cage adds little weight but catches wind, which [the balcony post](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/) covers.

## How does the kit split between a planter and the big pots?

The ten packets in the Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit divide neatly by weight. The five cool-season packets, kale, spinach, carrot, beet and turnip, grow in a sunny window or a balcony planter, so they carry little weight and can even stay indoors. The five warm-season packets, tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant and melon, need a big container and real sun, so they are the pots the balcony has to carry.

Tomato starts indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, pepper and eggplant 8 weeks before it, and cucumber and melon are sown outdoors once the soil is warm. Fill the big pots only when the seedlings move out. The box holds the seeds and the 24-page guide, so pots, mix and a trellis are yours to choose, and that choice decides the weight.

Our [apartment vegetable garden from seed](/blog/apartment-vegetable-garden-from-seed/) guide covers the indoor weeks.

Find your frost dates on the [state planting calendars](/planting/) and confirm them with your county extension office before you sow. Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99. A seed kit is the lightest thing on the balcony; the pots you put it in are the part to plan.

title: "Do You Need a Grow Light to Start Seeds in an Apartment?"
slug: "grow-lights-for-apartment-seedlings"
description: "When an apartment window is enough to start seeds, when it is not, and what a basic grow light setup looks like: a shop light, a timer and the right distance."
date: 2026-11-12
updated: 2026-11-12
eyebrow: "City apartment growing"
read: 7
answer: "You need a grow light to start seeds in an apartment unless you have an unobstructed south-facing window and are only growing quick greens. Tomatoes, peppers and eggplant spend six to eight weeks indoors and turn tall and floppy at a window. Give them a cheap LED shop light on a timer, 14 to 16 hours a day."
image: "media/2026-11/statics/blog-seeds-indoors.jpg"
image_alt: "Claymation scene: a small farmer character in a straw hat drops seeds into a tray of soil cells on a sunny windowsill, with leafy seedlings in clay pots behind him and snow outside the window"
image_caption: "A bright winter window starts the tray. Keeping the seedlings short for six weeks usually takes a lamp."
subtitle: "When a window is enough, when it is not, and what a basic light setup looks like in a small apartment."
kit_heading: "Which packets need the light"
about: "whether you need a grow light to start vegetable seeds in a city apartment, and how to set up a basic one"
faq:
  - q: "Can I start seeds in a south-facing window without a grow light?"
    a: "Sometimes: University of Minnesota Extension says an unobstructed south window may be enough to start seeds, but tomatoes and peppers, which need more time indoors, may become leggy without extra light. Greens sown in a pot that stays at the window usually manage. Slow warm-season crops usually do not."
  - q: "How many hours a day should a grow light be on for seedlings?"
    a: "Fourteen to sixteen hours a day on a timer is the usual advice. Iowa State University Extension says 14 to 16 hours, and University of Minnesota Extension says 16 to 18. University of Vermont Extension notes that plants need periods of darkness, so never leave it on around the clock."
  - q: "How far above seedlings should a grow light hang?"
    a: "Close: Iowa State University Extension puts most fluorescent fixtures 4 to 6 inches above the seedlings and LED fixtures a little higher, at about 8 to 12 inches. Raise the fixture as the plants grow. If the seedlings stretch toward the light, it is too far away."
  - q: "Will a regular LED shop light work as a grow light?"
    a: "Usually, yes, for seedlings: University of New Hampshire Extension says most seedlings can be grown to transplant stage under four-bulb T8 fluorescent shop lights. A bright white LED shop light rated near 6500K generally does the same job in a smaller, cooler fixture. Skip incandescent bulbs, which run hot and do little for plants."
  - q: "Do seeds need light to germinate?"
    a: "Most vegetable seeds in a beginner kit do not need light to sprout; they need warmth and moisture. Light matters from the moment the seedling breaks the surface. Check the tray daily and move it under the lamp as soon as the first stems appear, because a day of stretching in the dark is hard to undo."
  - q: "Does a grow light raise the electric bill much?"
    a: "A single LED shop light is one of the cheaper things in the apartment to run. The exact cost depends on your fixture's wattage, your hours and your utility rate, so check the label and your bill rather than a rule of thumb. The light runs for about ten weeks in late winter and spring, not all year."
---

This guide is for the apartment gardener with no balcony, and for the balcony gardener who starts seeds inside before the weather allows them out. In both apartments the question is the same: is the window enough, or do you need a lamp?

Here is how to tell, and what a simple setup looks like when the answer is a lamp. For what each window direction can grow on its own, read [which window direction is best for growing vegetables indoors](/blog/best-window-direction-for-growing-vegetables/).

## Do you need a grow light to start seeds in an apartment?

You need a grow light to start seeds in an apartment unless you have an unobstructed south-facing window and are growing only quick cool-season greens. University of Minnesota Extension's guide to [lighting for indoor plants and starting seeds](https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/lighting-indoor-plants) says a high-light spot may start seeds without artificial lighting. It adds that seeds that need more time indoors, such as tomatoes and peppers, may become leggy without extra light.

That is the whole answer in one sentence. Time indoors is what decides it, not the crop's size or its sun needs later on. Kale sown in a sill pot at a south window grows fine; a tomato seedling at the same window for seven weeks is a stretched, pale thing that falls over.

A North Dakota State University Extension agent describes the usual result in [Grow lights for seed starting](https://www.ag.ndsu.edu/news/columns/dakota-gardener/dakota-gardener-grow-lights-for-seed-starting). After many tries at starting seeds in south-facing windows, her seedlings were tall, thin and floppy, and she switched to lights. A city window with a building across the street gets even fewer hours of direct sun.

## Which seeds can start in a window, and which need a lamp?

Cool-season greens and roots can start in a bright window; the warm-season crops that spend six to eight weeks indoors need a lamp. The table sorts the ten varieties in the [Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit](/) by how long each one sits indoors, using the sowing timing for each variety.

| Packet | Time indoors before it goes out | Bright south window alone | With a grow light |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kale, spinach, beet, turnip | None required: direct sow in a sill pot or balcony planter | Works for baby greens | Faster, fuller leaves in winter |
| Carrot | None required: direct sow in a deep pot | Works, slowly | Works |
| Tomato (Floradade) | 6 to 8 weeks | Leggy | Short, stocky transplants |
| Pepper (Anaheim Chili), eggplant (Black Beauty) | 8 weeks | Leggy | Short, stocky transplants |
| Cucumber (Marketmore 76) | None: direct sow outdoors once the soil is warm | Not needed | Not needed |
| Melon (Honeydew Orange) | None, or 3 weeks indoors before transplanting | Workable for the short start | Works |

The honest version of the kit for an apartment runs like this. The five cool-season packets grow in a sunny window or a balcony planter, with or without a lamp. The warm-season five want a big container and real sun.

If that container is going on a balcony, check your lease or building rules and the balcony's weight limit first. A no-balcony reader starts them indoors and needs a balcony, a roof the building allows, or a community plot later. The box holds seeds, the guide and the box itself; the lamp, pots and soil are your shopping list.

If you have no balcony and no plans for an outdoor spot, you can skip the lamp entirely. Sow the greens at the window and leave the tomato and pepper packets sealed for a future season. [Growing vegetables from seed in an apartment with no balcony](/blog/apartment-vegetable-garden-from-seed/) walks through that plan.

## What a basic grow light setup looks like in a small apartment

A basic setup is one LED shop light, two short chains or a shelf to hang it from, a plug-in timer and a tray that fits underneath. University of New Hampshire Extension's fact sheet on [growing seedlings under lights](https://extension.unh.edu/resource/growing-seedlings-under-lights-fact-sheet) says most seedlings can be grown to transplant stage under four-bulb T8 fluorescent shop lights. A bright white LED shop light of similar length generally does the same job, runs cooler and weighs less, which matters on a rental shelf.

Hang the light from a bookshelf, a wire kitchen rack or a closet rod with the chains that come with the fixture. Put the tray on the shelf below and adjust the chain, not the tray, as the seedlings grow. Books under the tray work when the fixture cannot move.

University of Vermont Extension's [tips for choosing grow lights](https://www.uvm.edu/extension/news/tips-choosing-grow-lights) say a bulb rated near 6500K is ideal, because that matches natural daylight. The same page suggests a color rendering index above 85, and says seedlings need 16 to 18 hours of light a day at 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Color temperature is printed on most shop-light boxes and CRI on many, and most hardware stores carry a fixture that meets them.

Skip the dim purple lights sold as seedling kits. The UNH fact sheet measured one cheap purple LED that would have needed 34 hours of running time a day to give seedlings enough light, which is impossible. Incandescent bulbs are worse: NDSU Extension says they do not work well for starting seeds and generate a lot of heat.

## How far above the seedlings, and how many hours a day?

Keep fluorescent tubes a few inches above the seedlings, LEDs 8 to 12 inches above, and run the light 14 to 16 hours a day on a timer. Iowa State University Extension's answer to [how do I set up supplemental lights for my seedlings](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/how-do-i-set-supplemental-lights-my-seedlings) gives the distances. It says 4 to 6 inches for most fluorescent fixtures and about 8 to 12 inches for LEDs.

The same page sets the timer at 14 to 16 hours a day. University of Minnesota Extension says 16 to 18 hours for seedlings, so anywhere in that range is fine.

| Setting | Extension guidance | What to do in the apartment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hours per day | 14 to 16 (Iowa State); 16 to 18 (Minnesota) | Timer on at 6 a.m., off at 9 or 10 p.m. |
| Fluorescent distance | 4 to 6 inches (Iowa State) | Raise the chain every few days |
| LED distance | 8 to 12 inches (Iowa State) | Start at 8 inches; lift if leaves bleach |
| Darkness | Plants require periods of darkness (Vermont) | Never run the light all night |
| Temperature | 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit (Vermont) | Most heated apartments already sit there; keep the tray off a hot radiator |

The timer is the part people skip, and the part that makes the system work in an apartment. Without it, the light goes on when you remember and off at bedtime, so the seedlings get a short, uneven day that changes with your schedule. A mechanical plug-in timer from the hardware store solves it.

Watch the seedlings, not the ruler. If they lean and stretch, the light is too high or too weak; if the newest leaves look washed out, it is too close.

Iowa State also recommends air circulation around the seedlings to carry off the fixture's heat. A small fan on low does that, and gentle air movement is widely credited with sturdier stems.

## Timing: when the lamp goes on, and when it goes off for the year

The lamp goes on the day the first seedlings break the surface, and it goes off for the year once the last transplant has moved outside. Most vegetable seeds do not need light to sprout, so the tray can sit in a warm spot until then. From the first green loop of stem onward, every hour without strong light is an hour of stretching.

Count backward from your last spring frost to set the start date, and confirm that date with your county extension office before you sow. The [planting guide](/planting/) lists frost windows by state, and [when to start seeds indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/) covers the crop-by-crop schedule.

Where the last frost comes in late April or May, one light running from late February to mid May covers the tomato, pepper and eggplant packets. Shift that window to match your own frost date.

Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99.

The sowing timing for each variety tells you which three packets need the lamp, which two are sown straight into their outdoor containers, and which five can wait for the window. Add one shop light and a timer, and a studio apartment with a decent window becomes the nursery for the three packets that need a head start. The grown plants still need a big container and real sun outdoors.

---

A housewarming gift for a gardener has one job that other gifts do not: it has to wait. The person you are giving it to is living among boxes, does not yet know where the sun falls in the new yard, and may not know whether the soil is clay or sand. The best gifts are the ones that are still useful in three months, when the garden actually starts.

This guide sorts gifts by the home they moved into, because an apartment with a balcony and a house with a quarter acre need different things. Most ideas are under $25; a few are a little more. For gifts aimed at someone who is brand new to growing rather than someone who has moved, see [Gifts for New Gardeners](/blog/gifts-for-new-gardeners/).

## The one rule: give something that can wait

A gift that needs attention in the first week after a move is a chore, not a present. Live plants in particular suffer: they ride in a hot car, sit in a hallway with no light, and get watered when someone remembers. Seed, tools, pots and books keep without any care at all.

Seed in particular keeps for years when stored cool, dry and dark, so a seed kit given in November is still good when the ground thaws. That also means you do not need to time the gift to the planting season. Give it when the housewarming happens and let the recipient plant it when they are ready.

## For an apartment or a balcony

Give containers and seed that grows in them. A balcony garden fails when the pots are too small for the crop, so the gift should solve that. Two or three fabric or plastic pots, one of them 5 gallons, cover the fruiting crops; a window box or a 12 inch deep trough covers greens and roots.

Pair the pots with a seed kit that says what size pot each crop needs. Greens such as spinach and kale and roots such as beets and turnips are happy in 10 to 12 inches of soil. Peppers want 3 to 5 gallons, tomatoes, cucumbers and eggplant want 5 gallons, and a melon needs 10 gallons or more. [The Best Vegetables to Grow on a Balcony](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/) goes through sun, wind and watering for small spaces if you want to add a note.

A soil thermometer is the small extra that balcony growers rarely buy for themselves. Pots warm up and dry out faster than ground soil, and a thermometer tells them when the soil is warm enough for cucumbers and melons.

## For a rental with a small yard

Renters hesitate to dig, so give things that work above ground or come with them when they leave. A raised bed kit that assembles without tools is the generous option. A set of large fabric pots is the budget version and moves just as easily as the furniture.

With the bed or the pots, add seed for a first season. A kit with a mix of cool-season and warm-season crops gives them something to plant in early spring and again in late summer, which matters when they do not know yet how long they will stay. A kit that holds enough seed for a second sowing is better than one that is used up in one go.

## For a house with a real garden for the first time

This is the person who has never had ground to dig and is about to buy everything at once. Give the two tools they will use most: a hand trowel with a solid metal blade and a pair of bypass pruners from a maker that sells replacement blades. Cheap versions of both bend or jam in the first season.

Then give them the plan. A complete vegetable seed kit with a grow guide covers what to plant, how deep, how far apart and when, relative to their last frost date. The guide matters more in a new place than anywhere else, because the recipient has no experience of this yard's frost dates or soil. Whatever the guide says, tell them to confirm their frost dates with their county extension office; the [state planting pages](/planting/) on this site give a starting window for every state.

## For the plant lover who grows indoors

Not everyone who gardens has outdoor space, and a move often means a new set of windowsills. A grow light on a timer is the gift that makes a north-facing kitchen workable. A set of seed-starting trays with a clear dome lets them start tomatoes and peppers indoors in late winter, which is when a new garden really begins. [When to Start Seeds Indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/) covers the timing if you want to tuck a note in.

Seed still fits here. A kit's spinach, kale and beets grow on a bright sill, and the warm-season crops can be started indoors and moved out when the weather allows.

## What to skip

Skip a tender houseplant unless you know where it will sit and that someone will water it. Skip anything that assumes a yard: a wheelbarrow, a hose reel, a bag of compost. Skip gift cards to a nursery that is near their old home rather than their new one. Skip seed packets with no variety name, which tell the grower nothing about days to maturity or whether the crop fits a pot.

And skip the ornamental seed bomb or novelty kit that grows one marigold in a tin. It is a pleasant object, but it is not a garden, and a gardener will know the difference.

## How the Happy Seeds kit fits a housewarming

The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit is built for this exact moment. It is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99. The box slides open like a drawer, so it is ready to hand over without wrapping, and the guide gives a pot size for every crop, from the 12 inches a carrot needs to the 10 gallon container for the melon.

Five of the ten crops are cool-season and five are warm-season, so whichever month the move happens, there is something to plant within a few weeks of the ground being workable. And because it is seed, it keeps: a kit given at a November housewarming is ready for the first warm week of spring, after the recipient has found out where the sun lands in the new yard.

---

A seed kit for kids works when the first sprout appears before the child loses interest, and that is mostly a question of which crops are in the box. A kit full of carrots and peppers will test a six-year-old's patience for three weeks. A kit with spinach, cucumbers and beets shows green in a week and gives the child something to check every morning.

This guide covers which vegetables children grow best from seed, what to look for on a kit before you buy it, and how to run the project so it ends in a harvest rather than a forgotten pot. If you are choosing a kit for an adult beginner instead, [What to Look for in a Vegetable Garden Seed Kit](/blog/vegetable-garden-seed-kit-what-to-look-for/) covers the seven checks that matter there.

## The three things a kids' kit needs

Fast crops, big seeds and forgiving varieties. Everything else on the box is secondary.

Fast means the seed sprouts within about a week at room temperature. Big means the child can pick up one seed at a time and put it where it belongs. Forgiving means the plant survives a missed watering or a pot that gets knocked over. A crop that fails all three is a bad fit for a child, even if it is a fine vegetable.

The fourth thing is for the adult: a guide that says how deep, how far apart and when, in plain language. Children do the planting; adults do the timing. A kit whose only instructions are "plant in spring" leaves the adult guessing, and the adult's guess is usually what kills the project.

## Which vegetables children grow best from seed

The table ranks common garden crops for a child's project. "Days to sprout" is a typical range in moist soil at room temperature; cold soil slows everything down.

| Crop | Seed size | Days to sprout | Why it suits kids |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cucumber | Large | 5 to 10 | Big flat seeds, fast, grows visibly every day |
| Beans and peas | Large | 7 to 10 | Easiest seeds to handle; you can watch the seed split |
| Spinach | Medium | 5 to 10 | Fast, grows in a pot, ready to pick in 40 to 50 days |
| Beet | Medium, a cluster | 5 to 10 | Each "seed" is a cluster that sprouts several plants |
| Turnip | Small | 5 to 7 | One of the fastest sprouters in the garden |
| Kale | Small | 5 to 10 | Tough, keeps producing leaves after picking |
| Sunflower and pumpkin | Large | 7 to 10 | Big seeds, big results; not vegetables, but worth adding |
| Tomato | Small | 7 to 14 | Slower, but a cherry tomato is the harvest kids remember |
| Melon | Large | 7 to 10 | Fast sprout, but needs a 10 gallon pot and a long summer |
| Carrot | Tiny | 14 to 21 | Slow, tiny seedlings, hard to thin; a second-year crop |
| Pepper and eggplant | Small | 14 to 21 | Need warm soil and patience; start indoors with an adult |

Start with a crop from the top half. Once the child has seen a cucumber or a beet come up, carrots and peppers become a challenge rather than a disappointment.

## What to look for on the kit

Named varieties on every packet, so you can look up how long each one takes. A seed count, so you know there is enough to plant twice when the first pot gets overwatered. A germination rate printed on the packet, so that a tray of nothing is not the seed's fault. And a guide that gives depth, spacing and timing for each crop.

A kit with several crops is better than a single novelty packet for one reason: a child's first sowing often fails, and the second attempt is where the learning happens. Seeds in a cup are a pleasant afternoon. A kit with ten packets is a season. [What Does Germination Rate Mean on a Seed Packet?](/blog/what-germination-rate-means/) explains the number on the packet in terms you can share with an older child.

Skip kits that give no variety names, kits that are mostly flowers sold as "vegetables", and anything that promises a harvest in days. The fast part is the sprout; the harvest still takes weeks, and the guide should say so.

## How to run the project

Give the child one pot and one crop to own. A 10 to 12 inch pot of spinach or beets on a windowsill is the right size for a first project: small enough to check in a minute, big enough to produce something to eat.

Let the child plant by hand, with the adult reading the depth from the guide. Large seeds go about an inch down; small seeds such as kale and turnip go a quarter to half an inch. Cover, water gently, and put the pot where the child will walk past it every day.

Keep a sprout chart on the fridge. One tick per day, a drawing when the first sprout shows. This is the part that turns watering into a habit rather than a chore.

Thin when the seedlings crowd, and let the child do the pulling. Beets in particular need it, because each seed cluster sends up several plants. Thinnings of spinach, kale and beet are edible, which is the first harvest.

Outdoors, the timing follows the frost dates. Spinach, kale, beets and turnips can go out a few weeks before the last frost; cucumbers, tomatoes and melons wait until after it. Confirm your dates with your county extension office before planting; the [state planting pages](/planting/) on this site give a starting window for every state.

## How the Happy Seeds kit works for a child

The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit was built for adult beginners, and most of it suits a child's project with an adult alongside. It is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99.

Of the ten crops, five are good first projects for a child: Bloomsdale spinach, Marketmore 76 cucumber, Chioggia beet (the striped one, which is a surprise when it is cut), Purple Top White Globe turnip and Red Russian kale. All five sprout fast and grow in a pot. Floradade tomato and Honeydew Orange melon are the summer projects. Danvers 126 carrot, Anaheim pepper and Black Beauty eggplant are the patience crops, best kept for a second round.

Two honest gaps: the kit has no beans, peas or sunflowers, which are the easiest seeds of all for small hands. If you are putting together a kit for a young child, add a packet of one of those alongside it. And the guide is written for adults; you will be reading it to a child, not handing it over. For a six-year-old and a parent planting together, that is the right arrangement.

answer: "Harden off apartment seedlings over 7 to 14 days: begin with a few afternoon hours in shade on the balcony floor, then add sun and time each day. Bring them in at night until the last few days, and keep them inside on windy days or below 45 degrees F, 50 for peppers, eggplant and melon."
image: "media/2026-10/statics/glowup.jpg"
image_alt: "Claymation scene: a Happy Seeds Veggie Garden box on a sill by a window, three seedlings in terracotta pots, a blue watering can and a tomato character peeking from behind the box"

faq:
  - q: "How long does it take to harden off seedlings on a balcony?"
    a: "Plan on 7 to 14 days. Iowa State University Extension puts it at 7 to 10 days and the University of Minnesota Extension allows two weeks. Take the longer version when the weather is cold or windy, or when the balcony is high and exposed, and skip any day that is stormy."
  - q: "Can I harden off seedlings if I work all day?"
    a: "Yes, by stretching the schedule to two weeks. Do the first short, shaded days on a weekend. On workdays, leave the tray in a sheltered spot that stays shaded all day, and only when the forecast is mild and calm. Save the first days in the open for the second weekend, when you are home to watch."
  - q: "What temperature is too cold for seedlings on a balcony?"
    a: "University of Maryland Extension says not to put tender seedlings outdoors below 45 degrees F, and to leave indoor-raised cucumbers and melons out overnight only above 50. Illinois Extension advises planting eggplant when nights reliably stay above 50. Treat 50 as the limit for peppers too, and confirm frost dates with your county extension office."
  - q: "Do seeds sown directly in balcony pots need hardening off?"
    a: "No. A seedling that sprouts outdoors grows up in outdoor sun and wind, so it is already adjusted. Hardening off is only for plants raised indoors. Kale, spinach, carrots, beets, turnips and cucumbers are all sown straight into their balcony containers and skip the step."
  - q: "Can I harden off seedlings on a fire escape or a window ledge?"
    a: "No. A fire escape is an emergency exit, and most city fire codes require it to stay clear of anything that could block it. A tray on an outside window ledge can be blown off onto the sidewalk below. Use the balcony floor, where a gust can only tip the tray over."
  - q: "Do I need permission to put large planters on a rental balcony?"
    a: "Check before you buy the pots. Read the lease and the building rules, and ask the landlord or building manager about the balcony's weight limit, since several large containers of wet potting mix add up. Use saucers so water does not drain onto the balcony below."
---

This guide is for the apartment gardener with a balcony, a small terrace or a roof deck the building allows. It assumes a tray of seedlings that has only ever known a windowsill. Those seedlings cannot go straight outside: they need one to two weeks of short, lengthening visits first, a step called hardening off.

A balcony changes how that step works: there is no tree to sit under, the wind is often stronger than at street level, and the floor is concrete. If you have no outdoor space at all, start with [how to grow vegetables from seed in an apartment with no balcony](/blog/apartment-vegetable-garden-from-seed/).

## What is hardening off, and can balcony seedlings skip it?

Hardening off is the gradual exposure of indoor seedlings to outdoor sun, wind and temperature, and balcony seedlings cannot skip it. The University of Maryland Extension's page on [hardening off vegetable seedlings](https://extension.umd.edu/resource/hardening-vegetable-seedlings-home-garden) describes a change from soft, succulent growth to firmer, harder growth.

Iowa State University Extension's guide to [hardening and planting bedding plants](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/selecting-hardening-and-planting-bedding-plants) is plain about the risk: intense sun and strong winds may damage or kill tender seedlings. A balcony usually has more of both than a sheltered backyard. The basic method is in our post on [when to start seeds indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/); this guide adapts it to a balcony.

## When should apartment seedlings start going outside?

Start hardening one to two weeks before each crop's planting-out date: about the last spring frost date for tomatoes, and up to a week later for peppers and eggplant. Maryland Extension gives that one-to-two-week lead time. Find your frost date on the [state planting calendars](/planting/) and confirm it with your county extension office.

Not every crop makes the trip. The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit shows the split. Three of its ten varieties are started indoors, melon can be, and the rest are sown straight into their outdoor containers.

| Crop | How it reaches the balcony | Planting-out time | Hardening needed? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tomato (Floradade) | Started indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost | 1 to 2 weeks after last frost | Yes |
| Pepper (Anaheim Chili), eggplant (Black Beauty) | Started indoors 8 weeks before last frost | 2 weeks after last frost | Yes, on warm days only |
| Cucumber (Marketmore 76) | Sown straight into its balcony pot | 1 to 2 weeks after last frost, in warm mix | No |
| Melon (Honeydew Orange) | Sown in its pot, or started indoors 3 weeks before transplanting | 2 weeks after last frost, in warm mix | Only if started indoors |
| Kale, spinach, carrot, beet, turnip | Sown straight into a balcony planter | 2 to 6 weeks before last frost, by crop | No |

The five cool-season packets grow in a sunny window or a balcony planter. The five warm-season packets need a big container and real sun, which is why they end up outside. The box holds the seeds and the grow guide and nothing else, so trays, pots and potting mix are yours to add.

Cold decides the rest, and a frost date is only an average, so watch the forecast. Maryland Extension says not to put tender seedlings outdoors when temperatures are below 45 degrees F. Cornell's [tomato growing guide](https://gardening.cals.cornell.edu/garden-guidance/foodgarden/vegetable-growing-guides/tomato-growing-guide/) wants nights consistently above 45 before tomatoes are planted.

Eggplant needs more warmth. Illinois Extension's [eggplant page](https://extension.illinois.edu/gardening/eggplant) says to plant when nights reliably stay above 50 degrees F, and calls eggplant more easily injured by cold than tomato. Peppers are grown the same way, so hold peppers, eggplant and melon to 50.

## Where is the shaded, sheltered spot on a balcony?

The shaded, sheltered spot on most balconies is the floor against the building wall, at the hours when the wall or the balcony above shades it. Extension advice usually says to start seedlings under a tree or a covered porch. A balcony has neither, so watch where the shade actually falls in the afternoon before the first trip out.

Railings with open bars stop almost no wind, and a top-floor balcony or roof deck has no overhang for shade. Stand a cardboard box on its side with the opening facing the wall, weigh it down, and set the tray inside as a windbreak and sunshade in one. Keep trays off the railing and off any ledge, where one gust can send them over the edge.

Concrete is the other balcony problem. Virginia Cooperative Extension's guide to [vegetable gardening in containers](https://www.pubs.ext.vt.edu/content/dam/pubs_ext_vt_edu/426/426-336/SPES-796.pdf) warns about heat reflected from pavement and suggests raising containers so air can move beneath them. Set the tray on a board or an upturned crate, and check it twice on hot or windy days, because small cells dry out fast.

Never use the fire escape as the halfway house. It is an emergency exit, and most city fire codes require it to stay clear.

## A 10-day balcony hardening schedule

Most seedlings are ready in about ten days: two in shade, two with gentle sun, three of longer days in the open, then full days and nights. Iowa State puts the job at 7 to 10 days. The University of Minnesota Extension's guide to [starting seeds indoors](https://extension.umn.edu/gardening-minnesota/starting-seeds-indoors) allows two weeks, which is the better choice in a cold or windy spring.

| Days | Where on the balcony | How long | Bring the tray in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 2 | Floor against the wall, in shade, out of the wind | A few hours in the warm part of the afternoon | Before the evening cools |
| 3 to 4 | Same spot, moved to catch early-morning or late-day sun | About half the day | Before dusk |
| 5 to 7 | The open part of the balcony | Most of the day, with more direct sun each day | At night |
| 8 to 10 | Where the final containers will stand | All day, then overnight if nights stay above 50 degrees F | Only for cold, storms or strong wind |

Hardly anyone is home on a weekday afternoon to carry trays, so stretch the schedule to two weeks and anchor it on weekends. Do days 1 to 2 on a Saturday and Sunday. On workdays, leave the tray in a sheltered spot that stays shaded all day, and only when the forecast is mild and calm.

Save the first days in the open for the second weekend, when you are home to watch for wilting. Maryland Extension describes the same approach: a shaded, protected spot on warm days, in at night, and more sunlight each day.

Skip a day rather than push through bad weather. Maryland Extension says to keep tender seedlings in on windy days, and Iowa State says to move plants indoors if strong winds, a severe storm or frost threatens. This is where an apartment wins: the door is three steps away, and one rimmed baking sheet carries the whole tray.

Water a little less often during these days, but never let the plants wilt. Cornell notes that tomatoes are hardened by reducing water and fertilizer, not by exposing them to cold. Maryland Extension says melons and cucumbers raised indoors may stay out overnight only if it will not fall below 50 degrees F.

## How do you move seedlings into their final balcony containers?

Transplant in the evening or on a cloudy day, into containers that are already standing where they will stay. Iowa State gives that timing because it lets plants recover before they face direct sun. A large pot of wet mix is too heavy to shift later, so fill it in place.

Before the big pots go out, check your lease, the building rules and the balcony's weight limit, because several large wet containers add up. Put a saucer under each one. Virginia Cooperative Extension notes that water draining from an upstairs balcony can become a problem for the neighbors below.

Pot sizes for each crop are in [the best vegetables to grow on a balcony](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/). Set tomatoes deeper than they grew in the starter pot. Cornell says to bury the stem until the soil is just below the lowest leaves, and roots will form along the buried part.

Peppers and eggplant go in at the same depth they were growing. Add the stake or cage on planting day; Virginia Cooperative Extension advises giving supports while plants are very small to avoid root damage later. Water each plant in well.

## What do scorched, wilted or purple leaves mean?

Scorched leaves mean too much sun too soon, wilting means sun shock or thirst, and deep purple means cold; the fix for each is to go back a stage. White or tan papery patches on the leaves are sunscald. Those leaves will not recover, but new growth comes in normal if the tray goes back to shade for a couple of days.

Minnesota Extension says hardened-off plants may wilt when first exposed to full sun and generally recover within a day or so. Wilting in dry mix is simply thirst, so water and check the tray more often.

Purplish veins on tomato leaves are common and usually harmless. Clemson Cooperative Extension's [tomato factsheet](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/tomato/) notes that tomato foliage develops them as plants harden off. Leaves that turn deep purple all over point to cold, so keep the tray in on cool nights.

Snapped or flattened stems mean the wind got in, so rebuild the windbreak before the next trip outside.

A sunny balcony is what lets an apartment gardener grow the warm-season half of the kit as well as the greens and roots. Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99.

---

A stocking stuffer for a gardener has to pass two tests: it must fit in a stocking, and it must still be useful in spring. Most gift-shop garden items fail the second one. The ideas below are small, under $25 in most cases, and chosen because a gardener would buy them for themselves.

They are sorted by what they do rather than by price, because a beginner and a 30-year gardener want different things from the same stocking. For bigger gifts and full kits, the [seed gift guide](/blog/best-seed-gifts/) and [gifts for new gardeners](/blog/gifts-for-new-gardeners/) cover the rest of the list.

## What makes a good stocking stuffer for a gardener?

A good gardening stocking stuffer is small, durable and seasonless: it keeps in a drawer through winter and goes to work the first warm weekend. Durability matters more than looks, since the item will see dirt, water and sun. The cheapest versions of most garden tools are the ones that break, so one well-made thing beats three flimsy ones.

Usefulness is the second filter. A gardener already owns a trowel, so a second plastic one is clutter, while a soil thermometer or a tool-cleaning block fills a gap most people never buy for themselves. When in doubt, pick the consumable or the upgrade, not the duplicate.

## Seeds and seed-starting gifts

Seeds are the classic stocking stuffer for gardeners because packets are flat and light. Most vegetable seeds keep for several years in a cool, dry place. The one risk is choosing varieties they will not plant, which is why a kit with named varieties beats a random packet for anyone whose tastes you do not know.

1. **A complete vegetable seed kit.** Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99. The slide-out keepsake box sits beside the stocking or under the tree. The five cool-season packets can be sown in a pot on a sunny windowsill, while the warm-season five wait for a big container and spring sun.
2. **A single packet of something they love.** A gardener who grows the same tomato every year will plant a packet of it in a stocking without a second thought. Read the packet before buying; the post on [how to read a seed packet](/blog/how-to-read-a-seed-packet/) explains the packed-for date and the germination rate to look for.
3. **Seed-starting labels.** Wooden or plastic labels and a pencil solve the problem every seed starter has in March: six trays of identical green sprouts. A pack is a few dollars and disappears into any stocking.
4. **A soil thermometer.** The single most useful cheap tool for a seed starter, since warm-season seeds such as tomato, pepper, cucumber and melon will not germinate in cold soil. It tells the gardener when the bed is ready instead of guessing from the calendar.

## Hand tools that fit in a stocking

Small cutting and tying tools are the stocking stuffers gardeners reach for most, because they wear out or go missing every season. Look for metal where it matters and a brand the recipient would recognize, and skip anything with a painted floral handle.

5. **Bypass pruners.** A good pair is the top of the budget but the gift that lasts longest; bypass blades cut cleanly where anvil blades crush soft stems.
6. **Garden snips.** Lighter than pruners, for harvesting greens, deadheading and cutting twine; they fit a stocking toe.
7. **A hori-hori or a hand weeder.** A narrow, pointed blade for weeding, dividing and planting bulbs, and a tool many gardeners never buy themselves.
8. **A tool-cleaning block or oil.** A rust eraser and a small bottle of tool oil keep pruners sharp and closing smoothly. It is a gift for someone who already has good tools.

| Gift | Best for | Check before you buy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bypass pruners | Anyone with shrubs, tomatoes or roses | Steel blades, a locking latch, a brand they know |
| Garden snips | Balcony and vegetable growers | Spring-loaded, comfortable in a small hand |
| Hand weeder or hori-hori | Beds and raised beds | Full-tang blade, a sheath |
| Soil thermometer | Seed starters | Reads soil temperature, with a probe long enough to reach seed depth |
| Metal plant labels | Vegetable and herb gardeners | Weatherproof, with a marker or pencil |
| Gloves | Everyone | Fit; leather or nitrile palms; an extra pair |

## Gloves, labels, twine and the things that run out

Consumables are safe stocking stuffers because no gardener has too much twine, too many labels or too many gloves. These are the gifts to add if the stocking has room left after one good tool.

9. **Gloves.** Nitrile-coated gloves for seed starting and weeding, or leather palms for pruning; buy the recipient's size, not one-size.
10. **Metal plant labels.** Zinc or copper labels marked in pencil or paint pen last for seasons, where marker on a plastic tag fades within one.
11. **Jute twine.** A ball of natural twine ties tomatoes, cucumbers and peas to their supports and composts at the end of the season.
12. **Plant ties or clips.** Soft ties or small trellis clips are the thing a balcony tomato grower runs out of in August.

## Gifts for the gardener who has everything

For the gardener with a full tool shed, the best stocking stuffers add knowledge or comfort rather than another tool. These three suit the person who already grows well and would like to grow better.

13. **A pocket garden journal.** A small notebook for sowing dates, frost dates and what worked; gardeners who keep one plant better the next year. Add a note with their last frost date from the [state planting calendars](/planting/), and remind them to confirm it with their county extension office.
14. **A hand lens.** A 10x loupe shows aphids, seed structure and leaf disease a phone camera misses, and it costs less than a bag of potting mix.
15. **Gardener's hand soap or salve.** Pumice or coffee-ground soap and a plain hand salve are the one scented gift that gets used, because garden hands need it.

## What to skip in a gardener's stocking

Skip novelty tool sets, decorative items and anything that assumes a yard. Painted-handle tool sets bend on the first root; ceramic frogs and signs do nothing; a bulb planter is useless to someone who gardens in pots on a balcony.

Be careful with seeds for the wrong climate. Melons and peppers for a gardener in a short northern season, or spinach for a Florida summer, will sit in the drawer. When you do not know what they grow, a mixed kit with cool-season and warm-season crops covers both seasons.

Finally, do not buy the gift-shop "garden in a can" with no variety name and no seed count. A gardener will read the label, and a label that says only "tomato" tells them nothing. Named varieties, a seed count and a printed germination rate are the three lines that separate a seed gift from a novelty.

---

This guide is for the apartment gardener with no balcony, whose whole garden is a windowsill. In that apartment the limit is light, and the direction the window faces decides how much of it you get.

Here is what a south, east, west and north window can each grow from seed, and how to check what your own window really receives. For containers, soil and a 30-day sowing plan, start with [how to grow vegetables from seed in an apartment with no balcony](/blog/apartment-vegetable-garden-from-seed/).

## Which window direction is best for growing vegetables indoors?

A south-facing window with nothing blocking it is the best window for growing vegetables indoors. University of Missouri Extension's guide to [lighting indoor houseplants](https://extension.missouri.edu/publications/g6515) says windows facing south provide the brightest light for the longest duration. That holds across the United States, and the advantage is biggest from fall to spring, when the sun is low.

The University of Maryland Extension's page on [lighting for indoor plants](https://extension.umd.edu/resource/lighting-indoor-plants) sorts the four directions the same way. Its classes were written for houseplants and are given in foot-candles, a measure of brightness. The last column is our own reading of what each window can grow.

| Window faces | Direct sun | Maryland Extension's light class | What we would sow there |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| South | Around the middle of the day | High, 500 to 1,000 foot-candles; more with 4 to 6 hours of direct sun | Baby kale and spinach, beet and turnip greens, carrots in a deep pot; seedlings bound for outdoors |
| West | Afternoon | Medium-bright, 100 to 500; some west windows rate high | Baby greens, more slowly than south; watch summer heat at the glass |
| East | Morning | Medium-bright, 100 to 500 | Baby greens, more slowly than south; the sill stays cooler |
| North | Little or none | Low, 25 to 100 | Nothing worth cutting without a grow light |

Treat the numbers as rough. Illinois Extension's article on [houseplant light in winter](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/over-garden-fence/2021-12-20-make-sure-houseplants-get-enough-light-winter) gives lower figures: about 300 foot-candles for a south window and 150 for east or west. The order is the same in all three sources.

## What can you grow in a south-facing window?

A clear south-facing window grows baby greens from seed and, more slowly, carrots, and it is the best place to start seedlings for outdoors. Illinois Extension's guide to [growing herbs and lettuce indoors](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/good-growing/2017-11-17-grow-herbs-and-lettuce-indoors-winter) says those crops need 6 to 8 hours of bright light a day. It calls southern exposure windows great.

Kale, spinach, beet greens and turnip greens, cut young, should manage on the same light. Carrots need a pot 12 inches deep, so stand it on a table or plant stand tight against the glass.

A south window still will not carry a full-size tomato to harvest. The glass lets in a few hours of direct sun from one side, and a fruiting plant wants sun for most of the day. For those crops the window is only a nursery.

## Is an east- or west-facing window enough for vegetables?

An east- or west-facing window is enough for baby greens, though they grow more slowly than in a south window. Missouri Extension rates east and west windows as well suited to plants in the medium light range. East gets its direct sun in the morning and west in the afternoon.

The Illinois winter-light article offers a useful comparison: an east or west window is like standing about 5 feet back from a south one. Plan on smaller, slower harvests, and cut the leaves young. A pot of baby leaves is a realistic crop in medium light; a full-size kale plant is not.

West can rate a little brighter, and it runs hotter. Maryland Extension lists some west-facing windows in its high-light class, and afternoon sun arrives when the room is already warm. Illinois Extension's lettuce guide says room temperatures of 70 degrees F and below are best, so in a hot summer we would give spinach the east sill.

## Can you grow vegetables in a north-facing window?

Not from the window alone: a north-facing window gets little or no direct sun, and that is too little for vegetables. Missouri Extension says north windows are satisfactory only for plants requiring the lower light levels. Seedlings raised there stretch toward the glass and flop.

A north sill still works as the place where a grow light sits. Missouri Extension suggests 12 to 14 hours of lamp light a day where a window adds some light, and more where it adds none. Maryland Extension caps the total at 16 hours a day, because plants need a period of darkness.

Missouri's distance for fluorescent tubes is 6 to 12 inches above the plants. LED lamps vary, so follow the maker's instructions.

## How do you tell which way your window faces?

Open the compass app on your phone at the window or find the building on a map app, then watch when direct sun actually lands on the sill. The second check matters more in a city, where the compass can say south and the building across the street says otherwise.

| What you see on a clear day | Treat the window as |
| --- | --- |
| Direct sun on the sill from mid-morning to mid-afternoon | South |
| Direct sun in the afternoon only | West |
| Direct sun in the morning only | East |
| No direct sun, or a building or tree in the way all day | North |

Missouri Extension says to weigh a window's size, overhang, and shade from trees or buildings, and that the best windows are not shaded by any of them. Check again when the season changes. The winter sun is lower, so sun that clears the rooftop opposite in June can drop behind it in December.

Do not trust your eyes for brightness. Missouri Extension notes that the human eye is a poor judge of light intensity because it adjusts automatically. The plants are the better meter: Illinois Extension's post on [houseplants and indoor lighting](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/good-growing/2018-05-31-houseplants-and-indoor-lighting) says plants that stretch or look spindly are short of light.

## How do you get more light from the window you have?

Put the pots as close to the glass as they will sit without the leaves touching it, because light falls off quickly inside a room. Maryland Extension says light intensity decreases rapidly with increasing distance. Skip a sill that sits right above a hot radiator.

The glass itself matters. Maryland Extension lists curtains, insect screening, the season, shade from trees and buildings, and the cleanliness and type of window among the things that change light intensity. Wash the inside of the pane, tie back the curtain, and lift the insect screen in the cold months if your lease and window allow it.

Maryland Extension also notes that reflective, light-colored surfaces raise the light level in a room. A sheet of white card behind the pots bounces light onto their shaded side. Illinois Extension's lettuce guide says to rotate containers every few days.

Expect less in winter, when the same houseplant lighting post says light intensity is reduced and supplemental lighting may be needed. Keep the windowsill pots inside the window. Never move them onto a fire escape to chase the sun, because it is an emergency exit and has to stay clear.

## Which window is best for starting tomato, pepper and eggplant seeds?

The brightest south-facing window you have is the one for starting warm-season seedlings, and a grow light above them is better still. Missouri Extension's advice for stocky seedlings under fluorescent tubes is to place them within a few inches of the tubes once germination begins. Seedlings raised on window light alone often grow tall and thin.

The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit splits in two at the window. Its five cool-season packets (kale, spinach, carrot, beet and turnip) grow in a sunny window or a balcony planter. The five warm-season packets (tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant and melon) need a big container and real sun outdoors.

The box holds the seeds and the grow guide, so pots, potting mix and any light are yours to add. Tomato, pepper and eggplant only start at the window: sow tomato 6 to 8 weeks before your last spring frost, and pepper and eggplant 8 weeks before it. Cucumber and melon are sown outdoors once that frost has passed.

One to two weeks after the frost date, the seedlings move to a balcony container, a roof the building allows or a community garden plot. Before pots go on a balcony, check your lease, the building rules and the balcony's weight limit. Find your frost date on the [state planting calendars](/planting/) and confirm it with your county extension office.

The post on [when to start seeds indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/) covers the indoor weeks and hardening off. Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99.

faq:
  - q: "What vegetables can you grow indoors in an apartment without a balcony?"
    a: "Leafy greens and small roots: kale, spinach, lettuce, beet greens, turnip greens, radishes and carrots in a 12-inch pot. They tolerate the lower light of a window and fit in pots 6 to 12 inches deep. Tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, eggplant and melons need a large container and full outdoor sun, so they are a balcony or community-plot project."
  - q: "How much light does a windowsill vegetable garden need?"
    a: "Greens need about 6 to 8 hours of bright light a day, which usually means an unobstructed south-facing window. East and west windows give less; a north window is not enough on its own. Under a grow light, plan on 14 to 16 hours a day with the light 6 to 12 inches above the leaves."
  - q: "Can you grow vegetables in an apartment with only a north-facing window?"
    a: "Not well from the window alone. A north window gives soft, indirect light that keeps a houseplant alive but will not grow dense greens. Add an inexpensive full-spectrum LED on a timer for 14 to 16 hours a day and the same greens grow fine on a shelf anywhere in the room."
  - q: "Can you grow tomatoes indoors in an apartment?"
    a: "A full-size tomato is not an indoor crop. It needs a 5 gallon or larger container, direct sun for most of the day and room for a plant several feet tall. Start tomato seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost, then move the plant to a balcony, a roof the building allows, or a community plot."
  - q: "Is it legal to grow plants on a fire escape?"
    a: "In most cities, no. A fire escape is an emergency exit, and most city fire codes require it to be kept clear of anything that could slow a person climbing down. Pots on a fire escape can bring a violation for your landlord and put neighbors at risk. Keep the garden inside the window or on a real balcony."
  - q: "When should an apartment gardener start seeds?"
    a: "Greens for the window can be sown any month, since the room is always warm enough. For tomato, pepper and eggplant, count back 6 to 8 weeks from your last spring frost and sow then; cucumber and melon are sown outdoors a week or two after it. Confirm your frost dates with your county extension office before you plan."
---

This guide is for the apartment with a window and nothing else: no balcony, no patio, no roof access, maybe a landlord who frowns at drips. You can still grow real vegetables from seed in that space, but only certain ones, and only if you are honest about your light.

Here is what grows, how to judge the window you have, where the pots can sit, and a 30-day plan from sowing to the first cut of greens. If you do have a balcony, the companion post on [the best vegetables to grow on a balcony](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/) covers pot sizes, wind and sun hours.

## What vegetables can you grow from seed in an apartment with no balcony?

Leafy greens and small root crops are the vegetables that grow from seed in an apartment window; fruiting crops are not. Kale, spinach, lettuce, beet greens, turnip greens and radishes tolerate the modest light a window gives and fit in a pot under a foot deep. Carrots need a full 12 inches.

The University of Maryland Extension's guide to [growing microgreens and baby greens indoors](https://extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-microgreens-and-baby-greens-indoors) lists beets, kale, mustards, arugula and lettuce among the crops that grow acceptably in less-than-ideal light.

Tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, eggplant and melons are a different project. Each needs direct sun for most of the day and space for a plant that can reach several feet. A pepper wants a 3 to 5 gallon container; the others want 5 gallons or more.

A window does not provide that, so these crops get started indoors and finished somewhere outside.

| Crop | Grows in a window? | Container depth | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spinach, kale, lettuce | Yes | 6 to 8 inches | Cut young as baby greens; tolerate lower light |
| Beets (for greens) | Yes | 10 inches | Greens in a month; roots only with strong light |
| Turnips (for greens) | Yes | 8 to 10 inches | Fast greens; small roots possible in a bright window |
| Carrots (half-long types such as Danvers) | Yes, slowly | 12 inches | Need depth and patience; sow thickly, thin hard |
| Tomato, eggplant | Start only | 5 gallons or more outdoors | Need full sun and a large pot to fruit |
| Pepper | Start only | 3 to 5 gallons outdoors | Same sun; a slightly smaller pot |
| Cucumber, melon | Sow outdoors | 5 gallons with a trellis; melons 10 gallons or more | Vines and heat; neither suits a window |

The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit splits along the same line: its five cool-season packets (kale, spinach, carrot, beet and turnip) are the window crops. The five warm-season packets (tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant and melon) need a big container and real sun. The box holds only the seeds and the grow guide, so pots, mix and any light are yours to add.

## Which window is bright enough to grow vegetables?

A south-facing window with no building directly across from it is the one that grows vegetables; everything else needs help. Illinois Extension's guide to [growing herbs and lettuce indoors](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/good-growing/2017-11-17-grow-herbs-and-lettuce-indoors-winter) puts the need at 6 to 8 hours of bright light a day and names southern exposure as the best. East and west windows give roughly half a day of direct sun; a north window gives none.

City windows have a problem suburban windows do not: the building across the street. Stand at the sill at noon and again in mid-afternoon on a clear day and note whether sun is actually hitting the glass. If it is not, treat the window as north-facing no matter which way it points.

Illinois Extension estimates that each hour of natural light takes about 2 hours of supplemental light to replace. Lights should run 14 to 16 hours a day, held 6 to 12 inches above the leaves. A single full-spectrum LED strip on a timer covers one shelf of greens.

## Where do the pots go in a small apartment?

The best spot is a sill, a table or a shelf within about a foot of the brightest window, with a tray under every pot. Light drops off quickly as you move back from the glass, so a pot on the far side of the room is effectively in the dark. Rotate each pot a quarter turn every few days so the plants do not lean toward the window.

Weight is rarely a problem indoors, one real advantage over a balcony. [Maryland Extension](https://extension.umd.edu/resource/care-vegetable-seedlings) puts dry soilless mix at about 10 pounds per cubic foot, against roughly 75 for garden soil. Even watered, a 12-inch pot of mix is something a sill or a sturdy bookshelf can hold.

The concern in a rental is water, not weight: use saucers deep enough to catch a full watering and never let a pot sit in it.

Radiators are the other apartment constraint: Illinois Extension recommends room temperatures of 70 degrees F and below for greens, kept away from a direct heat source. Use the sill above a radiator for seed starting only. The warm spot speeds germination, but once the seedlings are up they want to move somewhere cooler and bright.

Never use the fire escape. It is an emergency exit, and New York's [Multiple Dwelling Law](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/MDW/53) and most other city codes require it to be kept clear of anything that could obstruct it. A pot out there is a violation for your landlord and a hazard for everyone above you.

## What containers, soil and water do indoor vegetables need?

Any container with a drainage hole and 6 to 12 inches of depth, filled with bagged potting mix, will grow greens and small roots. Illinois Extension is blunt about the mix: use a quality potting mix and do not use topsoil, which compacts, drains poorly and brings weed seeds and soil pests inside. Fabric pots, plastic nursery pots and window boxes all work; terracotta dries out fastest.

Water when the top inch of mix is dry, and water enough that a little runs into the saucer. Maryland Extension's guide to [vegetable seedling care](https://extension.umd.edu/resource/care-vegetable-seedlings) warns that a tray kept constantly wet invites damping-off, the fungus that topples seedlings at the soil line. Dry air from heating makes the opposite mistake easy too, so check pots daily in winter.

Maryland Extension notes that most potting mixes carry enough fertilizer for about 5 to 6 weeks of seedling growth. After that, greens you are cutting repeatedly benefit from a half-strength liquid feed every two weeks, and no more often than that. Microgreens cut at two to three weeks need no fertilizer at all.

## A 30-day starter plan for a window garden

Sow spinach and kale on day one, and you will cut the first baby greens around day 25 to 40, sooner under a light. Kale is up in about a week; spinach takes a week or two and prefers a cool room. Both regrow after cutting.

Carrots and beets go in the same day in a deeper pot and simply take longer.

| Day | What to do | What you should see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Fill pots, water the mix, sow spinach and kale a half inch deep, 1 inch apart; sow beets and carrots in the deep pot | Damp, level mix with the packet date on a label |
| 3 to 10 | Keep the surface moist; a sill above a radiator or the top of the fridge speeds things up | Spinach and kale sprouts; beets a little later; carrots last |
| 10 to 14 | Move sprouted pots to the brightest window or under the light; thin greens to about 2 inches apart | Short, sturdy seedlings; if they stretch, they need more light |
| 14 to 21 | Water when the top inch is dry; rotate pots; thin carrots to 2 inches | First true leaves; beet seedlings in clusters, thin to one |
| 21 to 40 | Cut spinach and kale leaves at 4 to 6 inches, leaving the center to regrow | A first small harvest; one or two more cuts to come |
| 40 to 60 | Mature greens; beets and turnips sized for greens, roots if the light is strong | Resow a second pot at day 21 so the supply does not gap |

Maryland Extension's timeline matches: baby greens at 4 to 6 inches by day 21 to 40, and mature greens past 6 inches by day 40 to 60. Cut plants give one to two more harvests. Sow a fresh pot every three weeks and the window stays in production.

## What about tomatoes and the other warm-season crops?

The warm-season crops are started indoors in the same window and then moved outside, so a no-balcony apartment is a nursery for them, not a home. Sow tomato 6 to 8 weeks and pepper and eggplant 8 weeks before the last spring frost. Cucumber and melon go into warm outdoor soil one to two weeks after it.

Find the date on the [state planting calendars](/planting/) and confirm it with your county extension office, because frost dates vary from neighborhood to neighborhood in a city.

Where they go after that is the real question. A community garden plot, a friend's yard, a shared roof the building has approved in writing, or a balcony in your next apartment all work.

For a balcony, check the lease, the building rules and the balcony's weight limit before a wet 5-gallon pot goes out. The post on [when to start seeds indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/) covers the indoor weeks and hardening off before the move.

If you only ever have the window, grow the five that belong there and give the other five packets to someone with a yard. That is a better outcome than a tomato dying on a sill in June. Happy Seeds is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99.
