Vegetable seed kits range from a handful of unlabeled packets in a cardboard sleeve to a curated box with a guide and tested seed. The box art rarely tells you which one you are holding. These seven checks do, and most of them take less than a minute on the product page or the back of the packet.

If you are still deciding between a kit and loose packets, [Seed Kit vs Seed Packets](/blog/seed-kit-vs-seed-packets/) covers that question first. This guide assumes you want a kit and need to tell a good one from a weak one.

## The seven checks at a glance

A good kit names its varieties, prints a germination rate, holds enough seed per packet and includes a real guide. It also uses non-GMO open-pollinated seed, says which crops grow in containers, and arrives ready to give. The table shows what to look for on each point and what should make you put the box down.

| Check | Look for | Walk away if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Variety count and mix | 8 to 12 crops, split between cool-season and warm-season | Only "mixed greens" or only summer crops |
| 2. Named varieties | A variety name on every packet, such as Marketmore 76 cucumber | Packets that say only "Cucumber" |
| 3. Seeds per packet | A stated total, around 50 to 150 per crop for a small garden | No seed count anywhere on the box or listing |
| 4. Germination rate printed | A percentage and a packed-for year on each packet | No rate, no date, or a "Below Standard" mark |
| 5. Guide quality | A booklet that covers timing by frost date, depth, spacing and care | A single card with "plant in spring" |
| 6. Non-GMO and open-pollinated | Both terms stated on the packaging | Vague claims like "natural" with nothing specific |
| 7. Container fit and gift-readiness | Pot sizes per crop; a box that needs no wrapping | Crops that need a large plot; packets loose in a bag |

The rest of the guide explains why each check matters and how to run it.

## 1. Variety count: enough crops to fill a season

Eight to twelve varieties is a practical range because a first garden needs crops for spring, summer and fall, not twelve kinds of tomato. Fewer than six leaves the garden empty for part of the year. More than fifteen is hard to plant in a raised bed or a few containers.

The mix matters more than the number. Cool-season crops such as spinach, kale, beets, turnips and carrots go in before the last frost and again in late summer. Warm-season crops such as tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant and melon wait until the soil is warm.

A kit that balances those two groups gives you early harvests from the greens while the fruiting crops take their time. The Happy Seeds Veggie Garden Seed Kit uses five cool-season and five warm-season varieties for exactly this reason. [What Are the Best Vegetable Seeds for Beginners?](/blog/best-vegetable-seeds-for-beginners/) explains the logic behind that split.

## 2. Named varieties: the crop name alone is not enough

Every packet should carry a variety name, because "tomato" could be a 55-day cherry or a 90-day beefsteak with very different needs. A named variety lets you look up days to maturity, disease resistance and whether it suits containers.

Named varieties also signal that the seed came from a real seed lot rather than a bulk bin. Catalog names like Danvers 126 carrot, Bloomsdale spinach or Black Beauty eggplant have decades of growing records behind them. If the kit's product page lists only crop names, ask the seller which varieties are inside before you buy.

## 3. Seeds per packet: more is not better

Fifty to 150 seeds of most crops is enough for a small garden. A kit that states its seed count is easier to trust than one that does not. A 4-by-8-foot bed might use a dozen beets, 10 kale plants and 2 or 3 tomato plants in a season, plus a short row of carrots sown thickly and thinned.

Full retail packets often hold hundreds of seeds of one crop, which is more than a beginner can plant before the seed ages. Kits usually size packets for a small garden instead. A box with 1,000 or more seeds across ten packets averages about 100 per crop, which covers a first garden plus a second sowing.

Check that the count is for the whole kit, not a single packet. "1,000 seeds" spread over ten packets and "1,000 seeds" in one packet of lettuce are very different kits.

## 4. A printed germination rate: the check most kits fail

A germination rate printed on the packet tells you how many seeds sprouted in a recent lab test. It is the single best sign that a kit sells tested seed.

Under [7 CFR 201.29](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/201.29), seed sold across state lines in packets of one pound or less need not show a germination percentage if it meets the federal minimum. A kit that prints the rate is volunteering information the law lets it skip.

The federal minimums themselves, set in [7 CFR 201.31](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/201.31), vary by crop. Any packet below the minimum must be marked "Below Standard" and show its actual rate.

| Crop | Federal minimum germination |
| --- | --- |
| Cucumber, turnip, lettuce, pea | 80% |
| Tomato, kale, melon (not watermelon), radish, squash | 75% |
| Beet | 65% |
| Spinach, eggplant | 60% |
| Watermelon | 70% |
| Carrot, pepper | 55% |

Alongside the rate, look for a packed-for year. A packet marked "packed for 2026" was packaged for this season rather than carried over from an earlier one.

Leftover seed still keeps for years when stored cool and dry; [Nebraska Extension](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g2090/na/html/view) lists typical storage life by crop. [What Does Germination Rate Mean on a Seed Packet?](/blog/what-germination-rate-means/) explains how to use the number when you sow.

## 5. Guide quality: the difference between a kit and a bag of packets

A real grow guide is what makes a kit worth more than its packets. The back of a packet has room for three lines, and a first season needs more than that. A good guide covers sowing time relative to your last frost date, planting depth, spacing, thinning, watering and what a healthy seedling looks like.

Judge the guide by page count and by whether it is specific to the varieties in the box. A 24-page booklet written for ten named crops is useful. A folded card that says "plant after danger of frost" is not.

Whatever the guide says, confirm your last and first frost dates with your county extension office before you plant. The [state planting pages](/planting/) on this site give a starting window for every state, including [New York](/planting/new-york.html) and [New Jersey](/planting/new-jersey.html). Local frost dates vary by several weeks within a state.

## 6. Non-GMO and open-pollinated: what the labels mean

Non-GMO and open-pollinated are the two labels that matter for a home garden kit, and they are not the same as organic or heirloom. Non-GMO means the variety was not genetically engineered. Open-pollinated means the plants are pollinated naturally and their saved seed grows true to type.

Hybrid seed is a deliberate cross between two parent varieties. According to [NC State Extension](https://caldwell.ces.ncsu.edu/news/a-guide-for-seed-buying/), hybrids will not produce consistent offspring from saved seed, while open-pollinated varieties can be saved if they are kept from crossing. Hybrids are not GMOs, but saved hybrid seed does not grow true, so you buy fresh seed each year.

Organic is a certification of how the seed crop was grown. It is a fine thing to look for, but it says nothing about whether the variety is named, tested or suited to a beginner. For a first garden, named open-pollinated non-GMO seed with a printed germination rate is the stronger set of claims.

## 7. Container fit and gift-readiness

A kit for a first garden should say which crops grow in containers and what pot size each needs, because many first gardens are a balcony or a patio. Greens and root crops are happy in 10 to 12 inches of soil. Peppers want a 3 to 5 gallon pot, tomatoes, cucumbers and eggplant want 5 gallons, and melons need 10 gallons or more.

If the kit's listing gives those sizes, the brand has thought about how beginners actually grow. If it does not, assume some crops will need ground space. [The Best Vegetables to Grow on a Balcony](/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/) lists which crops cope with small pots.

Gift-readiness is the last check, because seed kits are often bought for someone else. A box with a drawer or lid, a guide inside and packets that stand up on their own can be handed over as is. Loose packets in a plastic sleeve need a container and a card before they feel like a present.

## How Happy Seeds measures against the seven checks

Happy Seeds sells a kit, so it is fair to run the same seven checks on it. It is the complete first vegetable garden in one box: ten varieties, 1,000+ lab-tested non-GMO seeds, germination rate printed on every packet, a 24-page grow guide, $24.99. All ten varieties are named and open-pollinated, and every one comes with a container note, down to the 10 gallon pot the melon needs.

The packets sit in a slide-out keepsake box with a fabric pull tab. The full variety list and days to harvest are on the [facts page](/facts.html). Use the seven checks on any kit you are considering, including this one, and buy the box that answers every question before you open it.

---

Picking the right crops matters more than any tool or fertilizer when you are growing vegetables from seed for the first time. Some vegetables sprout in three days and shrug off cold nights and missed waterings. Others need two months of babysitting indoors before they can even go outside.

The ranking below leans toward crops that forgive mistakes, because a first garden is as much about learning the rhythm of sowing and harvesting as it is about the harvest itself.

## The easiest vegetables to grow from seed, ranked

Radish, leaf lettuce, spinach, kale, beets and turnips are the easiest vegetables to grow from seed because they are sown directly in the soil, sprout in under two weeks, and produce food within one to two months. Warm-season fruiting crops are a step harder, mainly because of timing, not skill.

The table ranks common first-garden crops from easiest to hardest. Days to harvest are typical ranges; the days listed "from transplant" assume you started seedlings indoors or bought them.

| Crop | Direct sow or transplant | Days to harvest | Container-friendly | Difficulty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Radish | Direct sow | 25 to 35 | Yes, 6 inches deep | Easiest |
| Leaf lettuce | Direct sow | 30 to 50 | Yes | Easiest |
| Spinach | Direct sow | 40 to 50 | Yes | Easy |
| Kale | Direct sow | 50 to 60 | Yes | Easy |
| Turnip | Direct sow | 50 to 60 | Yes | Easy |
| Beet | Direct sow | 50 to 60 | Yes, 10 inches deep | Easy |
| Bush bean | Direct sow after frost | 50 to 60 | Yes, 8 inches deep | Easy |
| Zucchini | Direct sow after frost | 45 to 55 | Large containers only | Easy |
| Cucumber | Direct sow after frost | 55 to 65 | Yes, 5 gallon with a trellis | Moderate |
| Carrot | Direct sow | 65 to 75 | Yes, 12 inches deep | Moderate |
| Tomato | Transplant | 60 to 80 from transplant | Yes, 5 gallon or larger | Moderate |
| Pepper | Transplant | 70 to 85 from transplant | Yes, 3 to 5 gallon | Moderate |
| Eggplant | Transplant | 75 to 85 from transplant | Yes, 5 gallon | Moderate |
| Melon | Direct sow after soil warms | 80 to 90 | 10 gallon or more | Harder |

Carrots sit in the middle of the list not because they are fussy once growing, but because their seed is tiny and slow, often taking 14 to 21 days to appear. Beginners frequently give up on a carrot row or let it dry out in the second week. Keep the soil surface damp and they will come.

Melons are last because they need a long, hot season and a lot of room. In a short-summer state they are a stretch for a first garden; in Texas or inland California they are much easier. Check the window for your state on the [planting calendar pages](/planting/) before committing space to them.

## Why cool-season crops forgive mistakes

Cool-season crops forgive mistakes because they germinate in cool soil, tolerate light frost, and give you a harvest before summer heat and pests arrive. Spinach, kale, beets, turnips, radishes and lettuce can all go in the ground two to six weeks before your last spring frost.

That early window is a safety net. If a sowing fails, you have time to sow again, and in most of the country you get a second chance in late summer for a fall crop. Spinach will bolt (send up a flower stalk and turn bitter) once days get long and hot, so treat it as a spring and fall vegetable rather than a summer one.

Cool-season crops also tend to be eaten as leaves or roots, not fruit. You do not have to wait for flowers, pollination and ripening; you simply pick when the plant is big enough. That removes several of the steps where a warm-season crop can go wrong.

## What to start indoors (and what not to)

Start tomatoes, peppers and eggplant indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost, and direct sow nearly everything else. Those three crops need a long warm season that most of the US cannot supply if the seed goes straight in the ground in May.

Everything else on the beginner list prefers direct sowing. Root crops such as carrots, beets and turnips dislike being moved and fork or stall if their roots are disturbed. Beans, cucumbers, zucchini and melons grow so fast that an indoor head start saves little, and their seedlings resent transplanting.

If you do start seeds indoors, the keys are a bright light source a few inches above the seedlings, warmth for germination, and a week of hardening off outdoors before planting. The full method is in [How to Start Seeds Indoors](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/).

## The three mistakes beginners make

The three mistakes that end most first gardens are sowing seed too deep, overwatering, and planting warm-season crops before the soil has warmed. Each is easy to avoid once you know to look for it.

**Sowing too deep.** A seed should be covered by only 2 to 3 times its own width. Lettuce and carrot seed want barely a dusting of soil; bean and squash seed can go an inch down. Buried too deep, small seeds run out of energy before they reach the light, and the packet gets blamed for poor germination.

**Overwatering.** Seedlings need the soil evenly moist, not soggy. Constant wetness starves roots of oxygen and invites damping off, the fungal collapse of seedlings at the soil line. Water when the top half inch is dry, and water less often but more deeply as plants grow.

**Planting warm crops too early.** Tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and melons sulk or die in cold soil, even if the air feels warm. Wait until one to two weeks after your last frost date, when soil is reliably warm, and you will often catch up to or pass plants that went in a month earlier. Your state's dates are on pages such as [New Jersey](/planting/new-jersey.html), [Texas](/planting/texas.html) and [California](/planting/california.html).

## A simple first-season plan

A good first garden has two or three quick greens, two or three root crops, and two or three warm-season fruiting crops, sown in that order across the spring. That spread teaches the full rhythm of a season while keeping the plant count manageable.

The ten varieties in the Happy Seeds kit were chosen on that logic: cool-season carrot, kale, spinach, beet and turnip, then warm-season tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant and melon, with a 24-page grow guide that walks through the timing. If you would rather assemble your own mix from individual packets, [this comparison](/blog/seed-kit-vs-seed-packets/) weighs the two approaches honestly.

Whichever route you take, read the germination rate on each packet before you plant. [What Does Germination Rate Mean on a Seed Packet?](/blog/what-germination-rate-means/) explains how to use that number to decide how thickly to sow.

Start with the forgiving crops at the top of the table, get one full cycle of sowing and eating under your belt, and the harder ones will feel far less intimidating next year.


---

faq:
  - q: "Is a seed kit cheaper than buying seed packets?"
    a: "Usually, per variety. A kit that includes ten packets for $24.99 works out to about $2.50 per packet, and you avoid paying shipping on several small orders or driving to find packets in stock. Per seed, large individual packets can be cheaper, but only if you actually plant that many seeds."

    a: "Kit packets are often smaller than full retail packets, which suits a small garden. A standard retail packet can hold hundreds of lettuce or carrot seeds, far more than a raised bed or balcony uses in a season. A kit with 1,000 or more seeds across ten crops covers a first garden with seed left over."

    a: "Good kits use the same named, open-pollinated varieties you would find in a catalog, such as Marketmore 76 cucumber or Bloomsdale spinach, and are held to the same US germination standards. Check that the kit names its varieties and prints a germination rate; avoid kits that list only the crop."

    a: "Yes. Store opened packets sealed in a jar in a cool, dry, dark place. Most vegetable seed stays viable for 2 to 5 years, though onion, parsnip and some lettuce decline faster. Do a quick paper-towel test before planting older seed so you know how thickly to sow."
---

Every first-time gardener hits the same fork: buy a boxed seed kit, or build a garden from individual packets off a rack or a catalog. Both can grow a fine first garden. The right answer depends on how much you already know, how much space you have, and whether anyone is giving this as a gift.

This comparison treats the two options fairly, including the cases where packets are clearly the smarter buy.

## How a seed kit compares to individual packets

A seed kit wins on curation, instructions, cost per variety and gifting, while individual packets win on choice, seed quantity per crop and flexibility for experienced gardeners. The table lays out the trade-offs for a typical first garden of about ten crops.

| Criterion | Seed kit | Individual packets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cost for ten varieties | One price; Happy Seeds is $24.99, about $2.50 per packet | Ten separate purchases, often plus shipping or a trip to the store |
| Seed quantity | Sized for a small garden; 1,000+ seeds across ten crops | Often hundreds of seeds per packet, more than a small garden uses |
| Variety choice | Fixed, pre-selected | Unlimited; thousands of varieties available |
| Curation for beginners | Crops chosen to work together across a season | You do the research on what suits your climate |
| Instructions | Usually a booklet covering the whole set | A few lines on the back of each packet |
| Gifting | Ready to wrap, no extra effort | Loose packets need a container or a card |
| Best for | First gardens, small spaces, gifts | Specific varieties, large plots, repeat gardeners |

Neither column is "better" in the abstract. The question is which trade-offs you are happy to make this year.

## Cost per variety, not cost per seed

Cost per variety is the fair way to compare, because a first garden needs ten different crops, not a thousand carrots. A kit priced at $24.99 for ten packets comes to roughly $2.50 per variety, and you pay once.

Buying ten packets individually means ten line items. Prices for single packets vary widely by company and crop, so we will not quote competitor numbers here, but anyone who has filled a cart at a big catalog seed company knows the total climbs quickly once shipping is added.

Cost per seed tells a different story. A full retail packet of lettuce or carrot can contain several hundred seeds, so the per-seed price is tiny. That only matters if you can use them, which brings us to waste.

## Most packets hold far more seed than a small garden uses

A standard retail seed packet usually contains far more seed than a raised bed or balcony garden plants in a season, and the surplus often expires before it is used. A single 4-by-8-foot bed might take 30 carrot seeds, a dozen beets, 10 kale plants and 2 or 3 tomatoes.

Leftover seed does keep. Stored cool, dry and dark, most vegetable seed remains viable for 2 to 5 years, as explained in [What Does Germination Rate Mean on a Seed Packet?](/blog/what-germination-rate-means/). But many beginners do not store seed well, and a half-used packet of spinach in a hot garage is simply money gone.

Kits sidestep this by sizing packets for a small garden. Across ten crops, 1,000-plus seeds is still more than a first garden needs, but the waste per crop is much smaller.

## Curation is the quiet advantage

Curation matters because the hardest part of a first garden is not planting, it is choosing. A rack of 300 packets offers no signal about which 10 will work together in your climate across a season.

A good kit solves that by pairing cool-season crops you sow in early spring (spinach, kale, beets, turnips, carrots) with warm-season crops you plant after frost (tomato, cucumber, pepper, eggplant, melon). You get a staggered season, early wins from the greens, and the summer fruiting crops that make the garden feel worth it. For the reasoning behind that mix, see [What Are the Best Vegetable Seeds for Beginners?](/blog/best-vegetable-seeds-for-beginners/)

The flip side is that curation removes choice. If you want a specific heirloom tomato or a purple carrot, a kit will not have it.

## Instructions: a booklet versus the back of a packet

Instructions are where kits pull furthest ahead, because a packet has room for a few lines and a kit can include a real guide. The back of a packet typically gives depth, spacing, days to maturity and a one-line sowing window.

That is enough for someone who already knows the difference between "direct sow" and "transplant." It is not enough for a first season. A kit guide, such as the 24-page grow guide in the Happy Seeds box, has space to explain timing relative to your frost date, what a seedling should look like at two weeks, and when to give up on a sowing and try again.

If you go the packet route, plan to supplement with a state planting calendar. The [planting pages](/planting/) on this site give sowing windows by state, including [New Jersey](/planting/new-jersey.html), [Texas](/planting/texas.html) and [California](/planting/california.html).

## Gifting: kits are built for it

Kits make better gifts because they arrive complete, look intentional, and ask nothing of the recipient at the moment of giving. A box with a guide inside can sit under a tree in December and be opened in March with everything the person needs to begin.

Ten loose packets in an envelope, however carefully chosen, read as a project rather than a present. If you are shopping for someone else, [The Best Gift for Someone Who Wants to Start a Garden](/blog/gifts-for-new-gardeners/) covers what to pair with seeds and what to write in the card.

## When individual packets are the better choice

Individual packets are the better choice for experienced gardeners, anyone who wants a specific variety, and anyone planting a large plot. In those cases a kit's curation is a limitation, not a help.

- You already know what grows well in your yard and want to repeat it.
- You want a particular variety for flavor, color, disease resistance or a short season.
- You are planting rows, not a bed, and need hundreds of seeds of one crop.
- You only need to refill one or two crops to round out seed you already own.

There is also a middle path. Many gardeners start with a kit in year one, learn which crops they actually eat and which thrive in their spot, and then switch to individual packets for the crops they want more of. That is a sensible way to spend a first season without overbuying.

## The short version

Choose a kit if this is your first garden, your space is small, or the seeds are a gift. Choose packets if you have gardened before, want specific varieties, or need volume. Either way, buy seed that names its varieties and prints a germination rate, and check your sowing dates against a local frost calendar before anything goes in the ground.

---
title: "What Does the Germination Rate on a Seed Packet Mean?"
slug: "what-germination-rate-means"
description: "Germination rate meaning explained: how to read the percentage on a seed packet, what US seed laws require, how to test seeds at home, and how long seeds last."
date: 2026-11-01
updated: 2026-11-01
eyebrow: "Seed basics"
read: 7
answer: "Germination rate is the percentage of seeds in a tested sample that sprouted under controlled lab conditions, so a packet marked 85 percent means roughly 85 of every 100 seeds should come up. Use it to decide how thickly to sow: the lower the rate, the more seeds you plant per spot."
image: "media/site/farmer/farmer-seeds.jpg"
image_alt: "Claymation scene: the Happy Farmer with a magnifying glass, inspecting giant clay sunflower seeds spilling from a burlap sack"
image_caption: "The rate on the packet is a lab result; the seedlings on the sill are what it predicts."
kit_heading: "Lab-tested, with the rate on the packet"
about: "seed germination rate"
faq:
  - q: "What is a good germination rate for vegetable seeds?"
    a: "Anything at or above the federal minimum for that crop is acceptable, and most fresh vegetable seed tests between 80 and 95 percent. Rates in the 70s are fine for direct-sown crops if you sow a little thicker. Below about 50 percent, it is usually cheaper and less frustrating to buy fresh seed."
  - q: "Does germination rate change over time?"
    a: "Yes, it falls as seed ages, and the decline speeds up with heat and humidity. The rate on a packet reflects the test done before packing, so a three-year-old packet will usually sprout at a lower percentage than printed. A home paper-towel test tells you where it stands now."
  - q: "What does 'packed for' mean on a seed packet?"
    a: "The packed-for date is the season the seed was tested and packaged to be sold in, for example 'Packed for 2026.' It is not an expiration date. Seed packed for a past season is often still good, but its germination rate will have drifted below the printed figure."
  - q: "How do I test old seeds to see if they are still good?"
    a: "Place 10 seeds on a damp paper towel, fold it over, seal it in a plastic bag, and keep it somewhere warm for 5 to 14 days depending on the crop. Count the sprouted seeds and multiply by 10 to get a rough percentage. Six or more sprouting means the seed is still usable."
  - q: "Why do my seeds germinate below the rate on the packet?"
    a: "Garden conditions are harsher than a lab. Cold soil, sowing too deep, crusted or dry soil, waterlogging and hungry insects all reduce emergence. A packet rate of 90 percent is a ceiling under ideal conditions; 60 to 80 percent emergence outdoors is normal and not a sign of bad seed."
---

That small percentage on the back of a seed packet is the most useful number printed there, and most beginners skip right past it. It tells you how many seeds to plant per spot, whether an old packet is worth sowing, and whether a seed company is being straight with you.

Here is what the number means, where it comes from, and how to check it yourself at the kitchen table.

## What germination rate means

Germination rate is the share of seeds that sprouted when a sample from the seed lot was tested under controlled temperature and moisture, expressed as a percentage. If a lab places 400 seeds on moist paper in a warm chamber and 352 produce a normal seedling, the lot's germination rate is 88 percent.

The test measures the seed itself, not your garden. In real soil, with cold snaps, crusting and insects, emergence will be lower than the printed rate. Think of the number as the ceiling, not a promise.

The practical use is simple. At 90 percent, sowing two seeds per spot and thinning to one is plenty. At 65 percent, sow three or four. For transplants, where every cell matters, sow two seeds per cell and snip the weaker one.

## Why US seed packets have to meet a minimum

US seed laws set minimum germination standards for vegetable seed, and seed that tests below the standard for its crop must be labeled as substandard or cannot be sold as ordinary seed. The Federal Seed Act and state seed laws also require truthful labeling of the kind and variety, the lot, and the test date or packed-for season.

The minimums vary by crop because some seeds are naturally harder to sprout than others. The standards are set at a level that assumes a reasonable, fresh lot, so a packet that meets them from a reputable source should perform well.

Most companies test above the minimum, and many print their actual tested rate rather than simply meeting the law. Happy Seeds prints the lab-tested germination rate on every packet in its kit, which lets you adjust your sowing density crop by crop instead of guessing.

## How to read a seed packet

A seed packet carries five pieces of information that matter: the lot number, the packed-for date, the germination rate, days to maturity, and planting depth. Everything else is nice to have.

| Field | What it tells you | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lot number | Which batch of seed this is | Reference if you have a problem; lots are tracked by the seller |
| Packed for | The season the seed was tested and packaged for | Not an expiry date; expect lower germination each year after |
| Germination % | Lab-tested sprouting percentage for the lot | Sow more seeds per spot as the rate falls |
| Days to maturity | Days from sowing (or from transplant) to first harvest | Check that your season is long enough; see the planting calendars |
| Planting depth | How deep to cover the seed | Usually 2 to 3 times the seed's width; shallow for tiny seed |

Days to maturity needs one caution. For crops normally transplanted, such as tomatoes and peppers, the number usually counts from transplant, not from sowing, so add the 6 to 8 indoor weeks when planning. The state pages under [planting calendars](/planting/) handle that math for you.

Variety name matters too. A packet that says only "Tomato" tells you nothing about size, days or disease resistance; one that says "Floradade" or "Marketmore 76" lets you look up exactly what to expect.

## How to do a paper-towel germination test at home

A paper-towel test takes ten seeds, a damp towel, a plastic bag and about a week, and it gives you a usable germination percentage for any packet you own. It is the same principle a seed lab uses, just at kitchen scale.

1. Count out 10 seeds (20 if you have plenty and want a finer result).
2. Dampen a paper towel so it is wet but not dripping, and lay the seeds on half of it.
3. Fold the towel over the seeds, slide it into a zip bag or lidded container, and label it with the crop and date.
4. Keep it somewhere warm, roughly 70 to 80 degrees F; the top of a refrigerator works.
5. Check daily, re-wetting the towel if it dries, and remove any seed that molds.
6. After the expected time, count the sprouted seeds and multiply by 10 for your percentage.

Expected times differ. Radish, lettuce, cucumber and brassicas show roots in 3 to 7 days. Tomatoes, beets and beans take 5 to 10. Peppers, carrots, parsley and spinach can take 10 to 14, so do not call them dead early.

Six or more out of ten is worth sowing, just a little thicker. Below five, buy fresh seed for anything you care about. You can even plant the sprouted test seeds if you handle the roots gently.

## How long seeds stay viable, by crop

Most vegetable seeds remain viable for 1 to 5 years, with onions and parsnips at the short end and tomatoes, cucumbers and brassicas at the long end. The ranges below assume cool, dry, dark storage; a hot garage or a humid basement can cut them in half.

| Crop | Typical viability | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onion, leek, parsnip | 1 to 2 years | Buy fresh each season if you can |
| Pepper, spinach, sweet corn | 2 to 3 years | Test before year three |
| Carrot, bean, pea | 2 to 4 years | Carrot germination drops noticeably after year two |
| Lettuce, beet, turnip, eggplant | 3 to 5 years | Beet and turnip are reliable keepers |
| Tomato, cucumber, melon, squash | 4 to 5 years | Among the longest-lived garden seeds |
| Kale, cabbage, broccoli, radish | 4 to 5 years | Store well in a sealed jar |

Storage is the variable you control. Fold the packet closed, put it in a sealed jar or tin with a packet of silica gel or a spoonful of dry rice, and keep it in a cool closet or the refrigerator. Seed kept this way will outperform the table; seed left in a shed will not.

## Putting the number to work

Use the germination rate to set your sowing density, use a paper-towel test to update it for older seed, and keep the packets you did not finish in a sealed jar for next year. Those three habits remove most of the mystery from "my seeds did not come up."

If you are choosing seed for a first garden, favor packets that name the variety and print a real tested rate; that transparency usually travels with other good practices. The crops that tolerate uneven germination best are covered in [What Are the Best Vegetable Seeds for Beginners?](/blog/best-vegetable-seeds-for-beginners/), and if you plan to start any of them indoors, the [step-by-step guide](/blog/when-to-start-seeds-indoors/) shows how to give each seed its best shot.


---

# Best seed gifts: 9 ideas that actually get planted

https://growhappyseeds.com/blog/best-seed-gifts/

Gift guide 
 The best seed gifts, ranked by whether they get planted. 
 By Happy Seeds · November 1, 2026 · 7 min read 
 Nine seed gift ideas for the gardener, the wants-to-be gardener and the person with one sunny windowsill, with the honest reason each one works or doesn't. 
 A seed kit is a gift that keeps going after the wrapping is gone. 

 The short answer The best seed gift is one the person can plant without buying anything else or looking anything up: a complete seed kit with several named varieties, instructions and a box worth keeping. After that, the strongest picks are a single-theme collection (salsa garden, salad bowl, herbs), plantable seed paper for the person who won't garden, and a seed-saving kit for the one who already does. Skip loose packets without instructions, novelty 'grow a rainbow' kits, and anything that depends on a yard the recipient doesn't have. 

 What makes a seed gift good? 
 A seed gift is good when it gets planted, and most of them don't. Seeds are cheap, light and easy to wrap, which is why they show up in stockings and gift bags every December. They are also easy to forget in a drawer until the packed-for date has come and gone. The difference between a seed gift that grows and one that doesn't usually comes down to three things. 
 
 Instructions that live with the seeds. A packet with a sentence on the back is not enough for a first-timer. A guide that says how deep, how far apart, how much sun and when to pick is what turns a packet into a plant. 
 A plan that fits their space. Someone in an apartment needs varieties that grow in pots on a windowsill or balcony. Someone with a yard can take the full range. 
 Something worth keeping. A gift that looks like a gift gets opened on the day and kept on a shelf. A handful of loose packets gets set aside with the wrapping. 
 
 Every pick below is rated on those three things, in rough order of how likely the gift is to end up as dinner. 

 1. A complete vegetable seed kit 
 The safest seed gift for almost anyone. A good kit bundles several named vegetable varieties, a grow guide and a box, so the recipient has everything except soil and a pot. It works for the beginner who has never grown anything, the lapsed gardener who needs a nudge, and the gift buyer who has no idea what to pick. 
 What to look for: varieties named with their cultivar (Tomato 'Floradade' tells you something; "tomato" doesn't), a germination rate printed on each packet, non-GMO and open-pollinated seed so they can save seed next year, and a guide that covers each variety rather than gardening in general. A kit built around ten reliable crops beats one with thirty packets nobody asked for. 
 That is the brief behind the Veggie Garden Kit from Happy Seeds: ten paper packets (1,000+ seeds) covering Tomato 'Floradade', Carrot 'Danvers 126', Cucumber 'Marketmore 76', Kale 'Red Russian', Spinach 'Bloomsdale', Beet 'Chioggia', Turnip 'Purple Top', Eggplant 'Black Beauty', Pepper 'Anaheim Chili' and Melon 'Honeydew Orange', a 24-page grow guide, and a slide-out keepsake box with the footprint of a paperback, so it wraps like a book. It costs $24.99, which works out to $2.50 a packet. Five of the ten (kale, spinach, carrot, beet, turnip) grow on a sunny windowsill or balcony planter, so it works for apartment people too. 

 2. A single-theme seed collection 
 Salsa garden, pizza garden, salad bowl, stir-fry mix. A themed collection of four to six packets is a fun gift for someone who already cooks and will understand why the varieties are together. It is less complete than a full kit (there is rarely a real guide), so it suits people who have grown something before. Check that the theme is honest: a "salsa garden" should actually contain a tomato, a chili and cilantro, not six kinds of pepper. 

 3. A culinary herb kit 
 Herbs are the right call for someone who cooks more than they gardens, or whose only growing space is a kitchen windowsill. Basil, parsley, chives and cilantro are quick, forgiving and useful within weeks. Look for the same things as a vegetable kit: named varieties, instructions per herb, and a container or box worth keeping. Happy Seeds has a Herb Garden Kit coming soon in the same keepsake box. 

 4. Plantable seed paper 
 Cards, gift tags, confetti and bookmarks made of paper with wildflower seeds pressed in. This is the seed gift for the person who will never run a vegetable garden but would happily tear up a card and water it. It is also the best add-on to another gift: a plantable tag on a wrapped box turns the wrapping into part of the present. It will not feed anyone, and the flowers that come up are usually a generic mix, so treat it as a token rather than a garden. 

 5. A seed-saving kit for someone who already gardens 
 If the person on your list already grows food, they do not need beginner seeds. Give them the kit for the next step: glassine envelopes, a seed-storage tin or box, labels, silica packets and a notebook for recording what they saved and when. Pair it with a packet of an open-pollinated variety they can save from. (Seed from hybrid plants does not come back true, which is the whole point of giving an open-pollinated one.) 

 6. A packet of something they can't buy locally 
 For the experienced grower, one unusual packet beats ten ordinary ones. A candy-striped beet, a purple-stemmed kale or an orange-fleshed honeydew is a conversation piece in a way that a standard red tomato is not. The gift is the story as much as the seed, so write the story on the tag: where the variety comes from, what it looks like cut open, why you picked it. 

 7. A seed gift for kids 
 Children want results fast and want to see something happen. Radish, lettuce, beans and sunflowers all sprout within days. The best kids' seed gifts come with big seeds that small hands can handle, a pot or cup to start them in, and a job to do every day (water, measure, draw). Skip anything with a plastic greenhouse that cracks the first week. A single packet of beans and a clear cup on a windowsill will outperform most boxed kids' kits. 

 8. A gift certificate or a grow-along 
 If you are not sure what they would plant, a gift card to a seed company lets them pick, and it ships instantly. The better version is a grow-along: give the seeds, buy the same packet for yourself, and plant together on a video call in spring. The seeds are the excuse; the gift is the company. 

 9. Seeds plus the one thing they are missing 
 The most useful seed gift is often seeds plus whatever is standing between the person and their first harvest. For an apartment, that is a 10-inch pot or a window box and a bag of potting mix. For a new homeowner, it might be a trowel and a watering can with a rose. For anyone, it can be a notebook. Keep the list short; one missing thing is a thoughtful gift, five is a chore. 

 What seed gifts to skip 
 
 Loose packets with no instructions. They are fine for gardeners and useless for everyone else. 
 Novelty kits that promise rainbows, giant pumpkins or "exotic" fruit. The seed is usually ordinary and the result is disappointment. 
 Anything that needs a yard the person doesn't have. Corn, winter squash and full-size melons want space. Give them to the person with a plot, not the one with a balcony. 
 Expired or unlabeled seed. If the packet has no packed-for date or germination rate, it has no way of telling you whether it will grow. 
 Seed with claims you cannot check. "Guaranteed harvest" is not a thing any seed can promise. Look for what a packet can actually state: variety name, germination rate, lot testing, non-GMO, open-pollinated. 
 

 How to pick by the person 
 
 Who it's for Best seed gift Why 
 Has never grown anything Complete vegetable seed kit Instructions and varieties chosen for reliability, nothing to look up 
 Apartment or balcony only Vegetable kit with windowsill crops, or an herb kit Kale, spinach, carrot, beet, turnip and most herbs grow in pots 
 Cooks a lot Herb kit or single-theme collection They will use what they grow 
 Already gardens Seed-saving kit or one unusual packet They have the basics; give them the next step 
 Won't garden, loves a nice object Plantable paper, or a kit in a keepsake box The gift is the thing itself 
 A child Big fast seeds (beans, radish, sunflower) plus a cup Results in days keep them interested 
 A housewarming Vegetable seed kit Fits any home and gives them a spring project; see gifts for new gardeners 
 

 When to give seeds 
 Seeds keep for a year or more in a cool, dry drawer, so timing is less important than people think. A kit given in December gets planted in March or April; a kit given in May can go straight into pots. The one thing to tell the recipient is the sowing window for what you gave them. For a vegetable kit, that is spring for the full set, and late summer for the cool-season crops if they want a fall round. Our guide to when to start seeds indoors covers the countdown from the last frost, and how to read a seed packet explains what the dates and percentages on the packet mean. For sowing dates where the recipient lives, see the planting calendars by state .

# Best vegetables to grow on a balcony or windowsill

https://growhappyseeds.com/blog/best-vegetables-to-grow-on-a-balcony/

Balcony growing 
 The best vegetables to grow on a balcony or a windowsill. 
 By Happy Seeds · November 1, 2026 · 7 min read 
 For apartment gardeners with a railing, a sill and a few pots: which vegetables fit, how big each pot needs to be, and how to keep them watered. 
 Three pots, one sill and a city view is enough. 

 The short answer The best vegetables to grow on a balcony are the ones that stay small and don't mind a pot: leafy greens like kale and spinach, root crops like carrots, beets and turnips, and, if you get six hours of sun, a tomato, a pepper or a cucumber in a bigger container. Greens and roots are happy in a pot 8 to 12 inches deep on a windowsill or in a railing planter. Fruiting crops need a 5-gallon pot or larger and full sun. Water pots more often than you would a garden bed, because they dry out fast. 

 How much sun does a balcony vegetable garden need? 
 Most vegetables want six hours of direct sun a day, and leafy greens get by on three to four. That one number decides what you can grow, so measure it before you buy a pot. On a clear day, step out at 9, noon and 3 and note where the light actually lands. The balcony above you and the building next door cast shade you won't notice until you look for it. 
 A south- or west-facing balcony usually gives you the six hours a tomato, pepper or cucumber needs. East-facing gets soft morning sun, plenty for greens and roots. North-facing is the hard case, and there's a section on it below. 
 Balconies have one thing a garden doesn't: walls. A pale wall bounces light onto the leaves. A dark wall soaks up heat and gives it back at night, which tomatoes love and spinach hates. 

 How do wind and heat change things on a balcony? 
 Wind dries a pot faster than sun does, so plan around it second. An eighth-floor balcony gets a steady breeze a backyard never sees, and it pulls water out of leaves, topples tall plants and snaps tomato stems heavy with fruit. 
 
 Put your heaviest, widest pots on the windy side to shelter the small ones. 
 Keep pots low and close together. A cluster shades its own soil and holds humidity. 
 Stake anything that will pass knee height on planting day, not the day it falls over. Tie the stake to the railing if you can. 
 Choose pots with some weight. A plastic pot of dry mix weighs almost nothing and will travel. 
 
 Heat is the other side of the coin. Concrete holds warmth, and a balcony can run several degrees hotter than the street. A dark pot in July can cook the roots along its sunny side. If your balcony bakes, use light-colored pots, or slip a dark pot inside a bigger pale one. 

 What size pot does each vegetable need? 
 Match the pot to the root, not the leaf. A spinach plant is happy in six inches of mix; a tomato wants a bucket. These are minimum sizes for the ten vegetables in the Veggie Garden Kit . Bigger is almost always better, because a bigger pot dries out more slowly. 
 
 Vegetable Minimum depth Pot size Plants per pot Sun 
 
 Spinach 'Bloomsdale' 6 to 8 in 1 gal, or a windowsill trough 4 to 6 per foot 3 to 4 hrs 
 Kale 'Red Russian' 8 to 10 in 2 to 3 gal 1 full size, or 3 to 4 for baby leaves 4 hrs or more 
 Carrot 'Danvers 126' 10 to 12 in 3 gal 12 to 16, thinned to 2 in apart 4 to 6 hrs 
 Beet 'Chioggia' 8 to 10 in 2 to 3 gal 6 to 8 4 to 6 hrs 
 Turnip 'Purple Top' 8 to 10 in 2 to 3 gal 4 to 6 4 to 6 hrs 
 Tomato 'Floradade' 12 in or more 5 gal (10 is better) 1 6 to 8 hrs 
 Pepper 'Anaheim Chili' 10 to 12 in 3 to 5 gal 1 6 to 8 hrs 
 Cucumber 'Marketmore 76' 12 in 5 gal plus a trellis 1 to 2 6 hrs or more 
 Eggplant 'Black Beauty' 12 in 5 gal 1 6 to 8 hrs, warm 
 Melon 'Honeydew Orange' 12 in or more 10 gal plus a trellis 1 Full sun, long season 
 
 
 For scale, a standard 10-inch pot holds about three gallons, and a 5-gallon bucket with holes drilled in the bottom is a fine tomato pot. Every container needs a drainage hole, and potting mix, not garden soil. 

 What are the easiest vegetables to grow on a balcony or windowsill? 
 The easiest balcony vegetables are kale, spinach, carrots, beets and turnips. They don't need pollinating or a trellis, they're fine with four hours of sun, and they fit in a railing planter or on a windowsill. 
 
 Kale 'Red Russian' has flat, blue-green leaves with purple veins and a more tender bite than curly kale. Pick the outer leaves and it keeps producing for months. It shrugs off frost, so it's often the last plant standing in fall. 
 Spinach 'Bloomsdale' is the fast one. Sow a pinch every two weeks for a steady supply of crinkled leaves. It bolts in summer heat, so grow it in spring and again in fall. 
 Carrot 'Danvers 126' is a medium-length carrot that copes with a pot better than the long kinds. Carrots are slow to germinate, two to three weeks sometimes, and the surface has to stay damp the whole time. That's normal. Once they're up, thin to two inches apart. 
 Beet 'Chioggia' shows candy-striped rings when you slice it. Each beet seed is a cluster, so thin the seedlings and eat the thinnings as greens. 
 Turnip 'Purple Top' is a two-for-one: peppery greens in a few weeks, then a purple-and-white root. In a pot, pull them small and sweet. 
 
 If you have six hours of sun and room for bigger pots, add the summer three. Tomato 'Floradade' is a determinate type: it grows to a set size and ripens over a few weeks instead of sprawling all season, which is what you want in a container. Pepper 'Anaheim Chili' stays compact and takes heat well. Cucumber 'Marketmore 76' is a vine, so give it a trellis tied to the railing and it climbs up instead of out. 
 All ten come in the kit, and the 24-page grow guide lists planting depth, spacing, watering and light for each one. The germination rate is printed on every packet, so you know how many seeds to sow per pot. 

 How often should you water vegetables in pots? 
 Water a pot when the top inch of mix is dry, which in summer means every day for a small pot and every other day for a 5-gallon one. Don't water on a schedule; water on a finger test. Push a finger in to the second knuckle. Dry means water now. 
 When you do water, keep going until it runs out the bottom, then stop. A quick splash wets the top inch and leaves the roots dry. Morning is best, so the plant has water on board before the heat. Keep a saucer under each pot, but tip it out an hour later so the roots aren't sitting in a puddle. 
 A few things make the rhythm easier: 
 
 Mulch the surface with an inch of straw or bark. It cuts evaporation sharply. 
 Group pots together. Shaded soil stays damp longer. 
 Go bigger. The most common reason a balcony tomato wilts is a pot that's too small. 
 Feed. Potting mix runs out of nutrients in six to eight weeks; a half-strength liquid feed every two weeks keeps fruiting crops going. In a heat wave, a potted tomato can drink a gallon a day. 
 

 What can a north-facing balcony still grow? 
 A north-facing balcony can still grow spinach, kale and turnip and beet greens, as long as it gets open sky and three or more hours of bright light. Skip tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and anything else that has to flower and set fruit. Grow for leaves, not roots, and pick them young. 
 Spinach 'Bloomsdale' and Kale 'Red Russian' are the two to start with. Sow them a little thicker than the packet says and cut the whole planter at three or four inches, like a salad mix. Turnip 'Purple Top' sown the same way gives mild, mustardy greens, and Beet 'Chioggia' gives red-stemmed baby leaves that look expensive in a salad. 
 Get every bit of light you can. Hang planters on the outside of the railing, where they clear the overhang, and prop white foam board behind the pots to bounce light back. Expect everything to take about half again as long as in sun. On an indoor windowsill, a south-facing window is roughly a partly shaded balcony; a clip-on LED grow light for twelve hours a day closes the gap for a tray of greens. 

 A small-space planting plan for one balcony 
 Here is a plan for a three-by-eight-foot balcony with six hours of sun: six containers, one windowsill, eight of the ten packets in the kit. 
 
 Railing planter, 30 inches long and 8 inches deep. Spinach 'Bloomsdale' in one half, Kale 'Red Russian' in the other. 
 Two 10-inch pots. Carrot 'Danvers 126' in one, Beet 'Chioggia' in the other, somewhere you'll remember to keep the surface damp. 
 One 5-gallon pot in the sunniest corner. Tomato 'Floradade', one plant, staked on planting day. 
 One 3-gallon pot beside it. Pepper 'Anaheim Chili', which likes the heat. 
 One 5-gallon pot against the wall, with a trellis. Cucumber 'Marketmore 76', trained upward. 
 Windowsill trough inside. Turnip 'Purple Top' sown thick for greens. 
 
 On timing: sow the greens and roots directly in their pots once nights stay above about 40°F, usually a few weeks before your last frost (the planting calendar for your state gives the typical frost window). Start the tomato, pepper and cucumber indoors six to eight weeks ahead of that frost and move them out once nights hold above 50°F; when to start seeds indoors walks through it. In late summer, pull the spent spinach and resow the greens and roots for a fall crop, covered in fall vegetables to plant in late summer . If this is your first garden of any kind, how to start a vegetable garden for beginners has the basics. 
 Start with the railing planter. Spinach in a trough is the fastest way to find out your balcony is a garden.

# Fall vegetables to plant in late summer: cool-season five

https://growhappyseeds.com/blog/fall-vegetables-to-plant-in-late-summer/

Fall sowing 
 Fall vegetables to plant in late summer: the cool-season five. 
 By Happy Seeds · November 1, 2026 · 6 min read 
 For gardeners who want a second harvest from the same bed or balcony, with a frost count-back table and five crops that do not mind the cold. 
 Kale on the sill: the easiest fall crop, sown in August. 

 The short answer Kale, spinach, carrots, beets and turnips are the fall vegetables to plant in late summer. Count back from your average first frost date: sow spinach and turnips 6 to 8 weeks before it, kale and beets 8 to 10 weeks before, and carrots 10 to 12 weeks before. They grow best as the weather cools, and a light frost makes most of them sweeter. 

 Why do cool-season vegetables like late summer sowing? 
 Because they grow up as the weather cools down, and cool weather is what they want. Kale, spinach, carrots, beets and turnips all germinate happily in warm soil, but they make their best leaves and roots when days are shorter and nights drop into the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Sow them in late summer and the timing works in your favor: the seeds sprout fast in the heat, then the plants mature in the mild, damp weather of early fall. 
 The same crops sown in late spring often go wrong. Spinach bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) the moment June heat arrives. Turnips get woody. A fall sowing avoids all of that, because the plants never meet a hot stretch at the wrong moment. Many leaf-eating pests also wind down by September, so a fall bed is usually cleaner than a spring one. 
 There is one more quiet benefit. The garden is already built. Your containers, your bed, your watering habit from summer: all of it carries straight into a second season without any setup. 

 When should I plant fall vegetables? Count back from first frost 
 Find your average first fall frost date, then count back the number of weeks each vegetable needs to mature, and sow on or before that date. Your local extension office or a quick search for "first frost date" plus your town will give you the average. In much of the northern United States that lands in late September or October; in the South it can be November or later. Our state-by-state planting calendars give the typical first-frost timing for your state. 
 The ranges below are typical for each vegetable type, not a promise for any particular packet. Add one or two extra weeks to the count, because growth slows as the days shorten. A crop that takes 50 days in June may take 60 in September. 
 
 Vegetable type Typical days to maturity Sow this many weeks before first frost 
 
 Spinach 35 to 45 days 6 to 8 weeks 
 Turnip 40 to 55 days 7 to 9 weeks 
 Kale 50 to 65 days (baby leaves sooner) 8 to 10 weeks 
 Beet 50 to 65 days 8 to 10 weeks 
 Carrot 65 to 80 days 10 to 12 weeks 
 
 
 So if your first frost is around October 15, carrots go in by late July, beets and kale by early to mid August, and spinach and turnips can wait until late August or the first days of September. If your frost is November 15, slide everything a month later. That is why "late summer" means something different in Minnesota than it does in Georgia. 

 Which vegetables should a beginner plant for fall? 
 Start with five: kale, spinach, carrots, beets and turnips. They are the classic cool-season crops, they all sow directly in the ground or a container (no transplanting), and they cover the two things fall does best, leaves and roots. These are also the five fall packets inside the Veggie Garden Kit , and the 24-page guide gives each one its own depth, spacing and watering notes. 
 
 Kale 'Red Russian'. Flat, blue-green leaves with purple stems, tender enough to eat raw when young. Pick outer leaves as you go and the plant keeps producing. If you only have room for one fall crop, this is the one. 
 Spinach 'Bloomsdale'. A crinkled, dark-leaved spinach that grows fast and tastes better after a cold night. Sow a short row every two weeks for a steady supply instead of one big flush. 
 Turnip 'Purple Top'. The fastest root in the group. Harvest at two or three inches across for the mildest flavor, and eat the greens too. 
 Beet 'Chioggia'. Red and white rings inside when you slice it. Each beet "seed" is a cluster that sprouts several seedlings, so thin them to about three inches apart. The thinnings are salad. 
 Carrot 'Danvers 126'. A sturdy, tapered carrot that copes with heavier soil better than the long, skinny types. Carrots are slow. That's normal. Seeds can take two to three weeks to show, and the roots need the longest run to frost of anything here, so sow them first. 
 
 If you are new to this, the beginner's guide to starting a vegetable garden covers soil, sun and watering basics that apply to any season. 

 How much frost can fall vegetables take? 
 All five handle a light frost (around 28 to 32 degrees Fahrenheit), and several of them taste better for it. Cold triggers the plants to store more sugar in their leaves and roots, which is why a kale leaf picked after frost is sweeter than one picked in August. 
 
 Kale and spinach shrug off light frost. Kale in particular keeps going well into cold weather, and in milder climates it stands through winter. 
 Carrots sweeten noticeably once the soil chills. The tops will wilt in a hard freeze, but the roots are fine underground for weeks. A layer of straw or shredded leaves over the row keeps the ground soft enough to dig. 
 Beets and turnips take light frost but not a hard freeze. Pull them once nights settle in the mid-20s. 
 
 A hard freeze (the mid-20s and below) is the real end of the season for leaves above ground. When it is in the forecast, pick what is ready and cover the rest with an old sheet overnight if you want a few more days. 

 How do I sow fall seeds when it is still hot out? 
 Keep the seedbed shaded and evenly moist until the seedlings are up. The hard part of a fall garden is not fall; it is August. The soil is hot and dries fast, and spinach in particular germinates poorly when the ground is above about 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Here is what works. 
 
 Water the bed or container deeply the evening before you sow, so the soil is cool and damp at the start. 
 Sow in the evening, a touch deeper than you would in spring (the packet depth plus a quarter inch is plenty). Deeper soil is cooler and holds moisture longer. 
 Shade the row. A piece of shade cloth, a board propped on bricks, or an old window screen laid over the bed all work. Remove it as soon as you see sprouts. 
 Water lightly every day until germination. A seed that dries out mid-sprout is finished, and this is the single most common reason a late-summer sowing fails. 
 Once the plants have a few true leaves, water deeply but less often, and mulch around them to keep roots cool. 
 
 For spinach, you can also chill the seed packet in the refrigerator for a week before sowing. It is an old trick and it helps more often than not. 

 Can I grow a fall garden in containers on a balcony? 
 Yes, and fall is arguably the best season to try it. All five of these crops suit a planter or a sunny windowsill, the weather is kinder to small pots than July is, and you will not be fighting the heat that bakes balcony containers in midsummer. 
 Use the deepest container you can for roots: 10 to 12 inches for carrots and beets, 8 inches for turnips. Kale and spinach are happy in 6 to 8 inches of soil. A standard window box grows a surprising amount of spinach. Put the planter where it gets the most direct sun you have, because as the sun drops lower in the sky through September, a spot that got six hours in July may get four. Containers also dry faster than ground beds, so keep checking them even when the air feels cool. For pot sizes and sun placement in more detail, see the best vegetables to grow on a balcony . 

 What if I missed the late-summer window? 
 Sow the same five crops in early spring instead. Kale, spinach, carrots, beets and turnips are two-season vegetables, and a spring sowing as soon as the ground can be worked gives you an early harvest before the heat arrives. In mild-winter regions you can often sow spinach and kale right through fall for a winter crop. 
 Spring is also when the full kit comes into its own. The other five packets, Tomato 'Floradade', Cucumber 'Marketmore 76', Eggplant 'Black Beauty', Pepper 'Anaheim Chili' and Melon 'Honeydew Orange', are warm-season crops that go in after the last spring frost, several of them started indoors first. If you are reading this in November, you have not missed anything. You are early, and when to start seeds indoors will help you plan the first sowing of the year.

---

# Gifts for new gardeners: what a beginner actually uses

https://growhappyseeds.com/blog/gifts-for-new-gardeners/

Gift guide 
 Gifts for new gardeners: what a beginner actually uses. 
 By Happy Seeds · November 1, 2026 · 7 min read 
 For anyone shopping for a friend, partner or parent who keeps saying they want to grow something: a short list that gets used, and a shorter list to skip. 
 A seed kit, house keys and a tomato who already feels at home. 

 The short answer The best gifts for new gardeners are the plain things they will reach for every week: a seed kit with a printed guide, a watering can with a rose, a small trowel, a few 10-inch pots or a window box, a bag of potting mix, gloves and a notebook. Skip gadgets and anything that assumes a yard they may not have. Match the gift to their space and the season, and you have given them a garden rather than a chore. 

 What do new gardeners actually use? 
 A new gardener uses about seven things in their first season: seeds, something to water with, something to dig with, something to grow in, soil, gloves and a place to write things down. Everything else is optional. That is good news for gift shopping, because every item on that list is easy to find and hard to get wrong. 
 Here is the list, with what each one is for and the detail that makes it a good one. 
 
 Gift What to look for Why it gets used 
 
 A seed kit with a guide Named varieties, a printed guide, enough seeds to try twice It is the gift that starts the garden. Loose packets with no instructions tend to sit in a drawer. 
 A watering can with a rose The rose is the sprinkler head on the spout. One to two gallons, removable rose Seedlings need a gentle shower, not a jet. A rose is the difference between watering seeds and washing them away. 
 A small hand trowel One-piece metal, a handle that fits their hand Potting up, digging holes, loosening soil. The tool they reach for every time. 
 Three or four 10-inch pots, or a window box Drainage holes and saucers Ten inches is big enough for a kale plant or a cluster of beets, and small enough to move. 
 A bag of potting mix Labeled for containers, not garden soil or topsoil The thing beginners forget to buy, right before they plant in dirt from the yard. 
 Gloves Snug fit, coated palms Thin enough to feel a seed, tough enough for wet soil and the odd thorn. 
 A notebook Small, plain, with a pen that lives in it Sowing dates, what sprouted, what the squirrels ate. Next year's plan starts here. 
 
 
 Give one of these and it is a nice gesture. Give three or four together and it is a garden in a bag. The seed kit is the piece that makes the others make sense, so if you only buy one thing, buy that. 

 Which seed kit makes a good gift? 
 A good gift seed kit has three things: named varieties, a real guide and a box worth keeping. Variety names matter because a beginner can look them up. "Tomato" tells you nothing. Tomato 'Floradade' tells you it is a compact, heat-tolerant tomato, which is something they can plan around. A guide matters because the back of a seed packet is small print with no context. And the box matters because this is a gift. A zip bag of packets does not feel like one. 
 That is the thinking behind the Veggie Garden Kit from Happy Seeds, and it is our pick for the seed-kit slot in a beginner's bundle. It holds ten named varieties, from Tomato 'Floradade' and Cucumber 'Marketmore 76' to Kale 'Red Russian' and Beet 'Chioggia', so there is something for a sunny yard and something for a windowsill. The 24-page grow guide covers planting depth, spacing, watering, light and harvest timing for each one, which means the person you give it to does not have to search for the basics. It comes in a slide-out keepsake box with the footprint of a paperback, so it wraps easily and sits on a shelf afterward. It is $24.99. 
 Whatever kit you choose, check two things on the packaging: that the varieties are named with their cultivar, and that there is a guide inside rather than a link to one. If you want to know what the fine print on a packet means, how to read a seed packet walks through every line. 

 What should you skip? 
 Skip anything the person cannot use in the space they have, and anything that does the gardening for them. That rules out most of what is sold as a gardening gift. 
 
 Gadgets. Soil meters, app-connected sensors, self-watering globes, seed dispensers. Most end up in the same drawer as the loose seed packets. A finger in the soil tells a beginner more than a meter does. 
 Big raised beds for renters. A raised bed kit is a fine gift for someone with a yard they own. For a renter it is a flat-pack problem: no place to put it, no permission to put it there, and no way to take it when they move. Give pots instead. 
 Tool sets with eleven pieces. They will use the trowel. The rest is weight. One good trowel beats a set. 
 Novelty kits. Grow-a-cactus tins and tiny greenhouse toys are fun for a week. Vegetables give the person a reason to go back out every day. 
 Anything that needs a yard they do not have. Hoses, wheelbarrows, lawn tools, long-handled anything. Ask where they will grow before you buy. 
 
 The test is simple: will this be in their hands in May? If you are not sure, it is probably a gadget. 

 How do you match the gift to their space? 
 Ask one question first: do they have a yard, or a window? The answer changes what you should buy more than anything else about them. 
 
 Their space Build the bundle around Leave out 
 
 Apartment with a sunny window A seed kit, a window box or two 10-inch pots, a small bag of potting mix, a one-quart watering can Raised beds, hoses, anything long-handled 
 Balcony or patio A seed kit, three or four pots with saucers, potting mix, a trowel, a one-gallon can with a rose Beds, large planters that cannot be moved 
 Rented yard A seed kit, pots, potting mix, trowel, gloves, a two-gallon can Permanent beds, fencing, trees 
 Yard they own A seed kit, trowel, gloves, a two-gallon can, a notebook, and if you want to go big, one raised bed Very little. This is the person who can use most things. 
 
 
 For the window and balcony gardeners, lean on the cool-season crops. Kale 'Red Russian', Spinach 'Bloomsdale', Carrot 'Danvers 126', Beet 'Chioggia' and Turnip 'Purple Top' all suit a planter on a bright sill, and they forgive a missed watering better than a tomato does. For the yard gardeners, the warm-season crops come into play: Tomato 'Floradade', Cucumber 'Marketmore 76', Pepper 'Anaheim Chili', Eggplant 'Black Beauty' and Melon 'Honeydew Orange' want room and full sun. Our guide to the best vegetables to grow on a balcony goes deeper on the small-space side. 

 Does the season matter when you give the gift? 
 Yes, but less than you would think, because seeds keep. A packet stored cool and dry at the back of a cupboard is fine for a year or more, so a seed kit given in December is ready for sowing in March. What changes with the season is what you say when you hand it over. 
 
 Winter (holidays). The seed kit is the whole gift. Add a note: start the tomatoes indoors in late winter; everything else goes out after the last frost. Pair it with the notebook, so they can plan while the ground is frozen. If they want a head start, when to start seeds indoors gives the timing, and the planting calendar for their state gives the typical frost dates. 
 Spring (Mother's Day, Easter, birthdays). The best time. Everything in a seed kit can go in the ground or in a pot within weeks. Add pots and potting mix so they can sow the same afternoon. 
 Summer (Father's Day, housewarmings). Too late for tomatoes from seed in most of the country, but exactly right for the cool-season five, which sow in late summer for a fall harvest . Tell them to hold the tomato packet for next year and start with kale and spinach now. 
 Fall. Spinach and kale can still go in a windowsill planter. The rest waits for spring, which is fine. Seeds are patient. 
 
 Carrots are slow. Melons are fussy. Tomatoes from seed take a couple of months before they look like anything. None of that is a problem if the person knows it going in, so write the honest version on the card. 

 What works for housewarmings, holidays, Mother's Day and Father's Day? 
 The same core gift works for all four occasions. What changes is the add-on and the note. 
 Housewarming. A seed kit is a housewarming gift that grows with the house. Pair it with one 10-inch pot and a small bag of potting mix, and they can plant the first packet before the moving boxes are unpacked. Suggest a variety on the card based on the home: kale for a sunny apartment, a tomato for a place with a yard. 
 Holidays. The kit fits in a stocking and under a tree, and it is still useful in April. Add gloves for a complete package. 
 Mother's Day. Mid-May is planting season almost everywhere in the country. A seed kit, a watering can with a rose and a window box is a gift she can use that weekend. If she already gardens, the notebook is the piece she probably does not have. 
 Father's Day. Mid-June is right for the cool-season crops and, in warm regions, a second sowing of cucumbers. A seed kit, a trowel and a two-gallon can. Pepper 'Anaheim Chili' is a good one to point him at: a mild chili that likes heat and looks impressive on the plant. 
 In every case, the card does half the work. A line like "start with the kale, it is the easiest" turns a box of packets into a plan, and a plan is what a new gardener needs most. If they want more than a line, how to start a vegetable garden for beginners is the long version.
